initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the granddaughter of his former governess
how_they_meet: Mrs. Braganza brings a birthday present to the Nath house and is snubbed by Raj's mother. Raj opens the gift the next day, goes to thank her in person, and Bobby answers the door; the article calls it love at first sight for him.
who_initiates: Raj, who engineers a second meeting at the library by deliberately mixing up their books
courtship_pattern: Quick, teenage and almost entirely unsupervised: a contrived book exchange, an attempt at the cinema, a party, a jealous rupture and a pursuit to Kashmir, all before either family is consulted.
emotional_dynamic: Uncomplicated mutual infatuation, tested once by her jealousy and thereafter directed outward at the fathers.
pair_conflict: Only one, and it is brief: Bobby sees Raj talking privately with his mother's dance partner and assumes he loves her.
pair_friction_explanation: The single misunderstanding over Nima is cleared as soon as Raj follows her to Kashmir. Nothing else divides them; from that point the couple is entirely united and every obstacle is external.
external_opposition_explanation: Raj's rich Hindu father abhors the match, accuses Jack of using his daughter's looks to trap a fortune, and offers a cash bribe to end it; Jack, insulted, forbids Bobby to see Raj and sends her to Goa. Raj is then pushed towards a marriage of business convenience, and the film ends in flight and a near-drowning.
lover_boy_explanation: The defining pure lover-boy role of his career and the film that created the persona. Raj has no ambition, occupation or project other than Bobby; the whole of his screen time is courtship, defiance of his father and flight, and the songs are built around him as a romantic figure.
chemistry_explanation: The article cites a contemporary review crediting the film's commercial appeal to its two fresh-faced young leads and praising the pair for acting with natural ease and freshness. That freshness is the point: both were teenagers, she was making her debut, and the unforced quality of the playing is what the film sells.
actor_transformation: A neglected boy raised by servants finds the first person who wants him for himself, and becomes capable of defying the father he had never challenged.
female_transformation: Bobby moves from a sheltered girl to one who leaves home for him, though the decisive acts at the close are largely his.
relationship_outcome: Reunited after the elopement collapses, with both fathers giving way.
romantic_songs: 'Main Shayar To Nahin', 'Hum Tum Ek Kamre Mein Band Hon', 'Jhoot Bole Kauwa Kaate', 'Na Mangoon Sona Chandi'
relationship_analysis: The template against which the rest of the filmography should be read. Friction between the lovers is deliberately near zero and almost every obstacle is imposed from outside, which is the structure Kapoor's romances return to for the next decade. The film also fuses three separate barriers, money, faith and parental will, into one wall, so that the couple's only available action is flight.
critical_reading: The film frames the fathers' objection as snobbery and treats the teenagers' certainty as self-evidently right, which still reads well. Less comfortable now is how little Bobby is given to do once the fathers take over: the confrontation, the bribe and the arranged counter-marriage are transacted between men, and her one decisive act, leaving with Raj, is taken at his prompting.

initial_relationship: Sweethearts before the film's main action
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article's summary begins with the attachment already formed and states only that Arjun loves Aarti and wants to marry her.
courtship_pattern: Undocumented in detail; the relationship exists before the plot and is destroyed by her father's decision rather than developed on screen.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual attachment defeated early, and thereafter a source of bitterness rather than of hope.
pair_conflict: None between them; the rupture is entirely her father's doing.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing in the article suggests conflict between Arjun and Aarti. She is married off against the attachment, and his later discovery of what has become of her is presented as her degradation rather than as a quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Aarti's father opposes the match outright and forcibly marries her to a man of his own choosing. The consequence, that Arjun later finds her working as a high-society call girl in another city, is the film's harshest statement of what the refusal cost.
lover_boy_explanation: Arjun's romantic identity is central to the film but it is a wounded rather than a courting one. He is defined by being refused and by what the refusal turns him into, which is closer to the tragic-lover register than to Bobby's ardent pursuit.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review discusses this pairing. The relationship is largely pre-history and aftermath rather than played out on screen, so there is little sustained interaction to assess, and its weight in the film comes from its absence.
actor_transformation: The loss confirms the village's reading of him as a bad character and pushes him towards the second attachment that destroys him.
female_transformation: Married against her will and later found working as a call girl, a decline the film attributes directly to her father's decision.
relationship_outcome: Ended by her forced marriage; they do not reunite.
relationship_analysis: The first of the two romances that bracket Arjun's story, and the one that establishes the film's argument that the village destroys what it refuses to understand. It is scored as a romance rather than as backstory because the whole of Arjun's subsequent behaviour follows from it.
critical_reading: The film uses Aarti's fall into prostitution as evidence against her father rather than as anything belonging to her, and she is given no voice in either the marriage or what follows. Read now, the most striking absence is her own account of any of it.

initial_relationship: College classmates
how_they_meet: As fellow students; the article describes Margaret as his Christian college mate, and the attachment forms after Aarti is married away.
courtship_pattern: A second love taken up in the wake of a first one lost, moving quickly to a decision to run away together.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and unusually equal at the end: she chooses to die with him rather than be left behind.
pair_conflict: None between them; the opposition is her family's and the catastrophe is Arjun's temper.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple is united throughout. The only violence in the relationship's vicinity is directed at the schoolmaster, and it is accidental.
external_opposition_explanation: Margaret's uncle and mother are against her marrying Arjun, which drives the couple to flee to the hills. The pursuit that follows produces the accidental killing of the one man who defended him.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is again his defining activity and he is willing to abandon everything for it, but the role's register is desperation rather than devotion, and the film ends in a joint suicide rather than in any romantic triumph.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. This is the first of many Kapoor and Neetu Singh pairings, and the article gives too little of the relationship to judge beyond the fact that her final choice is played as shared rather than as his decision alone.
actor_transformation: Finds a second attachment that briefly promises escape, then destroys it himself with a single unintended act.
female_transformation: Moves from a classmate to a woman who, asked whether she will come with him, jumps.
relationship_outcome: Both die by suicide after Arjun accidentally kills his teacher.
relationship_analysis: Unusual in the early filmography for ending in a shared death rather than a reunion, and for giving the woman the last consenting act. Placed against the Aarti thread, the film argues that Arjun is destroyed twice by other people's families, though the second time he supplies the fatal act himself.
critical_reading: A joint suicide framed as romantic transcendence is the reading the film wants; a modern one notes that Margaret is asked to die immediately after Arjun has killed a man, at the moment of his greatest distress, and that the film treats her assent as unproblematic.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records only that Raaja becomes enamoured of Rani.
courtship_pattern: Comic and confused, because she cannot tell Raaja from his identical twin; Ram eventually grows a moustache so that she can identify the brother she loves.
emotional_dynamic: Light and affectionate, played for the comedy of mistaken identity rather than for intensity.
pair_conflict: Her inability to distinguish the twins, which is a practical difficulty rather than a disagreement.
pair_friction_explanation: The only friction is the confusion between the brothers, and it is resolved cooperatively by Ram altering his appearance. Nothing divides Raaja and Rani themselves.
external_opposition_explanation: The bandit Sher Singh drives the plot and kills Ram, which suspends the romance, and Rani's father is present as a figure to be satisfied, but neither is directed specifically at the couple.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is genuine and produces a marriage, but Raaja's governing purpose is rescuing his sister and avenging his brother. Romance occupies the lighter half of a double role whose serious half is a revenge mission.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review discusses this pairing. The article gives the relationship only as a plot mechanism, and the material that survives is the identity confusion rather than anything specific to the two performers.
actor_transformation: Little; the marriage is the reward at the end of the mission rather than a change in him.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: They marry after the rescue, though the sister dies of her injuries.
relationship_analysis: A slight romance attached to a revenge thriller, notable mainly because the double-role device is aimed at the heroine rather than at the villain: the joke is that she cannot tell which brother she loves, and the solution is cosmetic.
critical_reading: Rani exists to be courted, confused and married, with no goal of her own and no consequence to her choices. The mistaken-identity comedy also sits awkwardly now, since it turns on a woman's inability to identify her own partner and is resolved by the men rather than by her.

initial_relationship: Fellow students; she is initially one of the two pranksters tormenting him
how_they_meet: At a Shimla college, where Ajay arrives as an easy target for Nisha and Vikram's pranks and becomes their friend after some initial hiccups.
who_initiates: Neither distinctly; the attachment grows out of a three-way friendship
courtship_pattern: Barely a courtship at all. The relationship forms through shared pranks and then through shared jeopardy once the two are suspects in a murder and have only each other to rely on.
emotional_dynamic: Companionable and practical, hardening into dependence as the danger closes in.
pair_conflict: None of substance; they disagree only over tactics, and both choose to go to the police.
pair_friction_explanation: The teasing that opens the film is directed at Ajay before they are a couple and is never hostile. Once the murder plot begins they act in complete concert, and the film offers no interpersonal quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Black Cobra kills their friend Vikram and the singer Sherie, steals the typewriter in order to frame them, and has them followed. The threat is sustained and lethal, though aimed at both of them rather than at the relationship as such.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor is the romantic lead of a college musical, but Ajay's function for most of the running time is to solve a murder he is accused of. The romance is assumed rather than pursued, and there is no courtship, rivalry or sacrifice for love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film is among the best remembered of the Kapoor and Neetu Singh comedies, and what carries it is an easy, unforced equality between the two rather than romantic charge; she is a full partner in both the pranks and the investigation.
actor_transformation: From the earnest outsider of the opening to one of a pair who depend on each other completely.
female_transformation: From a prankster with no stake in anything to a woman investigating a murder to save them both.
relationship_outcome: They clear themselves together and expose Black Cobra.
romantic_songs: 'Khullam Khulla Pyar Karenge', 'Ek Main Aur Ek Tu'
relationship_analysis: One of the clearest examples in the 1970s work of a romance built on partnership rather than pursuit, and a useful counterweight to Bobby. Female agency scores high because Nisha is a genuine co-investigator rather than a person to be rescued.
critical_reading: It has aged better than most of the decade's romances precisely because the courtship is so underplayed: there is no coercion, no stalking and no jealousy, and the woman is neither a prize nor a victim. The film's interest in the pair as a working team rather than as lovers is what keeps it watchable.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she believes him to be a woman in her band
how_they_meet: On a train to Kashmir, where Dev and his friend have joined a girls' singing band in drag to escape the gangsters who saw them witness a murder.
who_initiates: Dev, in his second disguise as the oil tycoon Esso
courtship_pattern: Conducted entirely through two simultaneous deceptions: he is beside her all day as the woman 'Devi' and courts her separately as a rich suitor called Esso, so every exchange is double.
emotional_dynamic: Comic and charged, with the charge coming from what she does not know rather than from anything between them.
pair_conflict: The deception itself; there is no quarrel, only the unexploded fact of who he is.
pair_friction_explanation: No genuine antagonism, but the relationship is built on a lie that must eventually detonate. The friction is structural rather than emotional, and the unmasking is played for comedy rather than for a rupture.
external_opposition_explanation: The gangsters hunting the two witnesses are the reason for the disguise and therefore the reason the courtship must be conducted falsely, but they are not aimed at the couple.
lover_boy_explanation: Courtship is the film's main activity and Kapoor plays it at full charm, inventing an entire wealthy persona to win her. It falls short of the top band because the romance is a comic engine rather than a devotion, and nothing is sacrificed for it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review discusses this pairing. Named in the main article among the films that fixed his romantic image, and the comedy depends on a light, quick rapport between the two that the drag premise would otherwise sink.
actor_transformation: From a man hiding inside two false identities to one accepted once both are stripped away.
female_transformation: Not documented; she discovers the deception rather than changing through it.
relationship_outcome: The disguises collapse and the article records that the romantic pairs remain intact.
relationship_analysis: The clearest early instance of a Kapoor romance driven by performance and disguise rather than by obstacle. Deception is total but entirely self-protective, which is why relationship health is scored in the middle band rather than low.
critical_reading: The film is a direct adaptation of Some Like It Hot and inherits its central problem: a courtship in which the woman is the only party who does not know who she is talking to. The 1975 framing treats this as farce; a modern reading notes that Ritu's consent is given to a person who does not exist.

initial_relationship: Sweethearts
how_they_meet: Not documented; the attachment exists when the film's conflict begins.
courtship_pattern: Not developed on screen; the relationship functions as the last and largest of the sacrifices Arun's father demands of him.
emotional_dynamic: Undocumented beyond the fact that giving her up is what finally breaks him.
pair_conflict: None between them; the renunciation is imposed by his father.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing in the article indicates conflict between Arun and Rekha. The relationship ends because he is told to end it for his brother's benefit.
external_opposition_explanation: Major Hemraj Sharma openly favours the twin Kewal and requires Arun to make sacrifices for him, including giving up the woman he loves. The demand is the immediate cause of Arun leaving home.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is something Arun loses rather than something he pursues. His defining activity is a struggle for a father's regard, and the renunciation registers as one more proof of favouritism rather than as romantic heroism.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review discusses this pairing, and the article gives the relationship in a single clause. There is almost no interaction recorded on which to judge it.
actor_transformation: Giving her up is the point at which obedience stops working for him and he leaves his father's house.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Ended by Arun's renunciation at his father's demand.
relationship_analysis: Included because the renunciation is load-bearing for the character even though the relationship itself is barely dramatised. It is the clearest early case of a Kapoor romance destroyed by a father rather than by a rival.
critical_reading: Rekha is a possession transferred between brothers at a father's instruction and is given no say in the article's account. The film's sympathy is entirely with the son who loses her, not with her.

initial_relationship: Old acquaintances; he had once talked her out of suicide
how_they_meet: They meet again after Arun leaves home, having first met when he saved her from killing herself.
who_initiates: Jyoti, who finds him work at her father's hotel
courtship_pattern: Built on practical rescue in both directions: he saved her life once, and she gives him a livelihood when he has nothing.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and reciprocal, the one supportive relationship in a film about a withheld father's love.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: The article records no disagreement. The relationship functions as refuge from the family conflict rather than as a source of any of its own.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is the father's hold over Arun's life rather than any objection to Jyoti; her own father employs him without difficulty.
lover_boy_explanation: A supportive attachment rather than a courtship. Arun's energies go to the confrontation with his father and the discovery that his mother is alive, and the relationship with Jyoti is the ground he stands on rather than the object of the film.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The mutual-rescue structure gives the relationship an equality unusual for the period, but the article carries too little of it to judge the playing.
actor_transformation: Finds outside his family the regard his father withholds, which is what allows him to confront the man at all.
female_transformation: From a woman he talked off a ledge to the person keeping him afloat.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends on rhetorical questions about the father.
relationship_analysis: A romance defined by reciprocal obligation rather than by pursuit, and the second of two in a single film. Read together with the Rekha thread, the film gives Arun one love taken from him by his father and one acquired entirely outside his father's reach.
critical_reading: Jyoti is unusually well placed for a 1975 heroine: she has a job to give, a father with a business and a prior claim on the hero's gratitude. The article's framing still subordinates her entirely to the father-and-sons story.

actress_prominence: Female lead of the younger generation
initial_relationship: College friends
how_they_meet: At college, where Pinky is his friend and the daughter of his father's doctor.
who_initiates: Not documented; the attachment is established as mutual
courtship_pattern: Settled and uncontested until it is interrupted, not by any obstacle of their own, but by the discovery of Pinky's parentage.
emotional_dynamic: Straightforward young love, used by the film as a bright counterpoint to the older couples' buried griefs.
pair_conflict: None between them; the crisis is Pinky's alone.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple never quarrels. The marriage is suspended because Pinky learns she was adopted and leaves to find her birth mother, which is a crisis of identity rather than a conflict with Vicky.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is the previous generation's concealed history: Pinky's illegitimate birth, her adoption, and the fact that her mother is the wife of the poet who once loved Vicky's mother. Nobody opposes the match directly.
lover_boy_explanation: Vicky is a romantic figure and the film is entirely about love, but he is fifth-billed in an ensemble and spends much of his thread waiting on someone else's discovery. Devotion is present; romantic heroism is not required of him.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review discusses this pairing specifically. The Kapoor and Neetu Singh rapport is used here as the film's lighter register against the Bachchan and Raakhee melancholy, and it works largely on their established ease.
actor_transformation: Little; he is constant throughout, and the change belongs to Pinky.
female_transformation: From a confident young woman to one who severs ties with her adoptive parents and goes looking for the mother who gave her up.
relationship_outcome: Reunited once the older generation's secrets are resolved.
romantic_songs: 'Tere Chehre Se Nazar Nahin', 'Pyar Kar Liya To Kya'
relationship_analysis: The junior romance in a two-generation film, and structurally the optimistic answer to the Amit and Pooja story: what the parents could not have, the children get. Vicky's own agency is limited, which is why lover-boy sits mid-scale despite a very high romance centrality for the film as a whole.
critical_reading: Pinky is given the film's most active younger-generation decision, to go and find her birth mother, and the film treats her illegitimacy with more sympathy than the period usually managed. Vicky's role in her crisis is mainly to wait, which reads now as a reasonable division rather than a failing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the daughter of the last man on his list
how_they_meet: In Madrid, where Bakshi runs a wine business; Anup begins falling for his daughter while hunting him.
courtship_pattern: Compromised from the start: he is drawn to her while pursuing her father, and the attachment ends with him kidnapping her to force Bakshi's hand.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine attraction running directly against the purpose that brought him there.
pair_conflict: He abducts her and uses her against her father, then abandons her.
pair_friction_explanation: The relationship contains a kidnapping and an abandonment. Whatever feeling exists is subordinated to the revenge, and he leaves her stranded on the road rather than take her with him.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father is the mafia lord Anup has come to kill, and he dies in the car chase that follows. The opposition is not disapproval but the fact that the romance and the mission cannot both survive.
lover_boy_explanation: Anup is a revenge protagonist, not a lover. He woos Bakshi's assistant Sapna purely for information, uses Seema as leverage, and surrenders to the police rather than stay with her. Romance is incidental to a role organised entirely around killing four men.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The article gives the relationship almost entirely in plot terms, and what it describes is instrumental rather than romantic.
actor_transformation: None; he completes the revenge and surrenders, and the attachment changes nothing.
female_transformation: Loses her father to the man she wanted to leave with, and is abandoned on the road.
relationship_outcome: He leaves her stranded and hands himself to the police; the article gives no reunion.
relationship_analysis: A useful outlier in the 1970s run: Kapoor in a revenge thriller where the romance is a tool and the hero walks away from it. The low lover-boy score against a high billing shows how far the persona could be set aside when the genre required it.
critical_reading: Two women are used instrumentally here, Sapna for information and Seema as a hostage, and the film treats neither as a wrong requiring redress. Read now, the hero's surrender is framed as moral resolution while the abduction of the woman who loved him goes unremarked.

initial_relationship: Not documented
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article refers to Madhu only as his love.
courtship_pattern: Not documented; the relationship is named rather than dramatised in the article's summary.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented.
pair_conflict: Not documented; the pressure on the relationship comes from his concealed identity and his criminal foster-father.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is recorded. The threat to the relationship is that he is living under a dead man's name while the man who raised him as a weapon hunts him.
external_opposition_explanation: Laxman Dada raised him from a kidnapped child specifically to destroy the father he does not know he has, and pursues him when he runs. Any life with Madhu depends on escaping that design.
lover_boy_explanation: The article poses the question of whether he will manage a new life with Madhu as one of the film's open questions, which places the romance among his stakes without making it his defining activity. The role is organised around identity and revenge.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review discusses this pairing and the article gives the relationship in a single clause. There is not enough recorded interaction to judge it.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the article's plot ends before any resolution.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article closes with the question of whether he will begin a new life with Madhu.
relationship_analysis: Scored thinly because the article's plot section ends in rhetorical questions rather than a resolution. The pairing is recorded because the relationship is explicitly one of the stakes the film sets up, but almost every field is undocumented.
critical_reading: Too little survives to read the film's framing of the relationship, beyond noting that Madhu is positioned as the reward for successful reform rather than as a participant in it.

initial_relationship: Childhood sweethearts from feuding clans
how_they_meet: As children at the madarsa, where Qais writes Laila's name on his slate instead of God's; they meet again as adults in the marketplace of her town when he comes to buy camels.
who_initiates: Neither; the bond is presented as pre-existing and supernatural
courtship_pattern: Secret meetings in childhood, forcible separation, then secret meetings again as adults, until a killing ends any possibility of union.
emotional_dynamic: Absolute and mutual to the point of the physical: when one is hurt, the other bleeds.
pair_conflict: None whatever; the lovers are never divided from each other.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no interpersonal conflict at any point. The film's entire dramatic pressure is external, and the pair's unanimity is the premise from which everything else follows.
external_opposition_explanation: Two clans, the Amaris and Sharwaris, who cannot conceive of being joined by love rather than blood; a father who withdraws Laila from school to protect her reputation; her brother Tabrez, who kills Qais's father and is killed in turn; exile; and her marriage to Prince Bakhsh. The opposition is total and ends in death.
lover_boy_explanation: The definitive lover-boy role of the filmography alongside Bobby, and in some ways its purest form: Qais has no identity apart from loving Laila, loses his name to become Majnu, abandons society entirely and wanders the desert for a single sight of her. Nothing else remains of the character.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses the pairing. The film's power rests on the mutuality of the obsession being credible, and Madan Mohan and Jaidev's songs carry much of that work; the role remains the best-known screen Majnu of its generation.
actor_transformation: From a boy who cannot write God's name for thinking of her to a man who has dissolved entirely into the love, losing his name, his home and finally his reason.
female_transformation: Married to a prince who promises to keep his distance until he can replace Majnu in her heart, which he never does.
relationship_outcome: Death; the article records that when Bakhsh finally understands the nature of their love, it is too late.
romantic_songs: 'Hussn Hazir Hai', 'Tere Dar Ko Chhod Chale', 'Likhe Jo Khat Tujhe'
relationship_analysis: The extreme case of the pattern that runs through the whole early filmography: pair friction at zero, external opposition at maximum. Where Bobby resolves that structure happily, Laila Majnu carries it to its logical end, and the two films together define the range of Kapoor's romantic persona in the 1970s.
critical_reading: The film presents self-annihilating love as the highest value, which is the legend's own framing and is hard to argue with on its terms. A modern reading notices that Laila is married off, contained and largely static while Majnu's suffering is the spectacle, and that the prince who respects her refusal is treated as an obstacle rather than as the one man who asks her consent.

actress_prominence: Female lead opposite Kapoor; one of three heroines
initial_relationship: Acquainted; he courts her at the hospital where she works
how_they_meet: At the hospital, where Akbar comes to romance Dr. Salma Ali; the article introduces them already attached, with her father the obstacle.
courtship_pattern: Public, performed and comic: he serenades her in qawwali, and the pursuit is conducted in songs rather than in private scenes.
emotional_dynamic: Light, teasing and mutual, played against her father's disapproval rather than against any doubt of hers.
pair_conflict: None of substance between them.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple is aligned throughout. Such friction as exists is between Akbar and her father Taiyyab Ali, who is the target of the film's most famous comic number.
external_opposition_explanation: Salma's grumpy father Taiyyab Ali disapproves of Akbar and is the standing obstacle to the match, though the film treats him comically rather than as a real threat.
lover_boy_explanation: Akbar is the most romantic of the three brothers and carries the film's courtship songs, but he is one of three leads in a plot about a family's reunion, and the romance is a strand rather than the spine. Devotion is real; the film's demands on him lie elsewhere.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses the pairing. This is among the most enduring of the Kapoor and Neetu Singh pairings, and the qawwali sequences do most of the work, giving the courtship a performed, public charm that the film's other romances lack.
actor_transformation: Little; Akbar is constant, and the film's transformation is the family's restoration rather than his.
female_transformation: Moves from a daughter under her father's authority to a woman who marries against it.
relationship_outcome: They are united as the family is restored.
romantic_songs: 'Parda Hai Parda', 'Tayyab Ali Pyar Ka Dushman'
relationship_analysis: The clearest example of a Kapoor romance conducted through music rather than through plot: the courtship exists almost entirely in two qawwalis, and the relationship's texture is public performance. Romance centrality is mid-scale because the film belongs to the three-brother structure, not to this pairing.
critical_reading: The courtship is consensual, mutual and good-humoured, which has aged well. 'Tayyab Ali Pyar Ka Dushman' is a public humiliation of the heroine's father staged as a crowd-pleaser, and it is the one element that reads more uncomfortably now than it did.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the daughter of the man he believes has wronged him
how_they_meet: Rajesh approaches Kajal deliberately, having been told a false story that her father Kishorilal kidnapped a man's son, and pretends to love her in order to extort the diamonds.
courtship_pattern: A sequence of engineered meetings conducted under a false pretence, complicated by Kajal's existing attachment to her childhood love Sanjay and by a rival scheme running alongside his.
emotional_dynamic: Asymmetric and dishonest at the outset: her feeling is real, his is a manoeuvre.
pair_conflict: The courtship is a deception, and she is attached to another man throughout.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no open hostility, but the relationship rests on a lie and on a prior claim: Kajal loves Sanjay, and Rajesh's approach is a scheme. The friction is built into the premise rather than expressed in quarrels.
external_opposition_explanation: Saudagar Singh's false story is what sets the courtship in motion, and he later uses Kajal directly to get the diamonds. Her attachment to Sanjay is the other standing obstacle.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor is the top-billed romantic star of a musical, but the character courts as a means to an end and is not the man Kajal ends with. The lover-boy apparatus, songs and charm, is fully deployed in the service of a fraud.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film's reputation rests on its Nasir Hussain musical surface and on R. D. Burman's score rather than on this relationship, which the plot keeps deliberately insincere.
actor_transformation: Abandons the scheme and helps rescue her, which is the film's correction of his opening position.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond being rescued and paired with Sanjay.
relationship_outcome: The deception collapses; the article states that Sanjay and Kajal become a couple while also pairing Rajesh off, and does not reconcile the two statements.
romantic_songs: 'Kya Hua Tera Vaada', 'Bachna Ae Haseeno', 'Hai Agar Dushman'
relationship_analysis: One of the few 1970s Kapoor romances in which he is the deceiver rather than the wronged party, and in which the heroine ends with another man. The article's own confusion about the final pairings is preserved rather than resolved.
critical_reading: A courtship begun as a plan to abduct and extort is treated by the film as a forgivable misunderstanding once the hero changes his mind, and Kajal is never shown learning what he originally intended. 'Bachna Ae Haseeno' has outlived the film, which makes the framing easy to forget.

initial_relationship: Employer and employee; he hires her into his advertising agency
how_they_meet: Karan offers Nisha, a gifted advertising woman who became a recluse after her lover Shashi died, a job at his agency, and she accepts.
who_initiates: Karan professionally; Nisha emotionally, because he resembles the man she lost
courtship_pattern: Not a courtship but a drift, conducted inside a workplace and against his recent marriage, with the older woman's attachment resting on a resemblance rather than on him.
emotional_dynamic: Unequal and displaced: she is attached to a dead man's likeness, and he to an attention his marriage does not give him.
pair_conflict: He is newly married, and she wants him for what he resembles rather than for who he is.
pair_friction_explanation: The relationship is founded on a substitution neither can acknowledge, and on a marriage it violates. The article stops before any confrontation, so the friction is latent rather than dramatised.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is internal to the triangle: Karan's wife Timsy. There is no family or social force ranged against them.
lover_boy_explanation: Karan is the object of an older woman's transferred devotion rather than a pursuer, and the film is interested in what he represents to her. There is no courtship, no rebellion and no sacrifice for love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The premise requires Kapoor to be credible as a revenant of Shashi Kapoor's character, which the casting arranges neatly, but the article's four-sentence summary leaves the playing undocumented.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the article's summary ends once the triangle is established.
female_transformation: Emerges from reclusion into a workplace and an attachment, though to a substitute.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: The most psychologically unusual romance of Kapoor's 1970s work, and the only one in which he is cast as a living reminder of someone dead. Notable also as one of several films in which he and Shashi Kapoor appear together; Shashi's own workbook records this film as a cameo with a Tragic lovers pairing, the other side of the same triangle.
critical_reading: The film's interest in a woman's grief and in an older woman's desire was unusual for 1977 and gives Nisha real interiority. What is undocumented is whether the film ultimately punishes her for it, since the article carries no account of the ending.

initial_relationship: Recently married
how_they_meet: Not documented; the marriage is established when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None shown; the film begins after the wedding and is concerned with what happens to the marriage rather than how it was made.
emotional_dynamic: A young marriage with a third party inside it almost immediately.
pair_conflict: His growing attachment to Nisha.
pair_friction_explanation: The strain is entirely the husband's attachment elsewhere. The article does not record open quarrels, so this is scored on the situation rather than on dramatised conflict.
external_opposition_explanation: The pressure comes from inside the triangle rather than from families or society; nobody opposes the marriage itself.
lover_boy_explanation: In this relationship Kapoor plays a husband whose attention is elsewhere, which is the opposite of the lover-boy function. There is no courtship and no devotion on display.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The casting relies on the audience's familiarity with Kapoor and Neetu Singh as a couple, which the film then uses as the settled marriage being threatened.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented; the article's summary does not follow Timsy past the setup.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: Recorded as a separate pairing because the marriage is the thing the film puts at risk, and because it inverts the usual Kapoor and Neetu Singh dynamic: here their established warmth is the status quo rather than the goal.
critical_reading: Timsy is positioned as the injured party without being given much to do about it, at least within the article's account. The film's sympathy appears to lie with the two people in the affair rather than with the wife.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Manohar, a tourist guide, meets Savitri while she is teaching music, falls for her at the first meeting, and follows her home on the pretext of selling her eggs.
courtship_pattern: Begins as ingratiating comedy, with a fake egg-selling pretext she sees through immediately, and turns after her marriage into a campaign of proximity and threat.
emotional_dynamic: Initially mutual and warm; after the marriage it curdles into her open hatred of him.
pair_conflict: He offers to kill her husband, reasoning that the astrologer has given the man forty days anyway, and then befriends the husband to demonstrate that he could.
pair_friction_explanation: The article states plainly that his offer to kill Sagar begins her hatred of him, that she tells him to stay out of it, and that he responds by entering the household to show he could act at any time. This is sustained coercion directed at her, not an external obstacle.
external_opposition_explanation: Savitri marries Sagar at her critically ill mother's insistence, and the astrologer's prediction that her husband will die within forty days hangs over everything. Sagar's wealth and his family's proposal are what take her out of Manohar's reach.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is the whole of Manohar's function and he pursues with the full lover-boy apparatus, but the pursuit turns coercive, which is the opposite of the archetype's devotion. Scored mid-scale to record that the romantic identity is total while the conduct disqualifies it from the upper band.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The early egg-selling courtship is played as charm and the later scenes as menace, and the interest of the pairing is that the same performer supplies both.
actor_transformation: From an engaging suitor into a standing threat against the woman he claims to love.
female_transformation: From a woman falling in love with him to one who protects her husband from him and finally exposes him.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's summary breaks off during Sagar's confrontation with Manohar.
relationship_analysis: The most important corrective in the early filmography to the lover-boy reading. Where Bobby and Laila Majnu score zero to two on pair friction with maximal external opposition, this film puts the friction inside the relationship and makes the Kapoor character its source. It is the first clear instance of the persona being turned against itself.
critical_reading: The film's own framing keeps Manohar sympathetic as a thwarted lover, but the plot it describes is a man who proposes murdering a woman's husband and then moves into their house to remind her he could. Savitri's response, refusing, protecting Sagar and finally telling him, is the most decisive female action in the batch, and the film gives her the moral position throughout.

initial_relationship: Acquaintances; he is her father's former pupil
how_they_meet: Raju, an old student of the schoolmaster Chintamani Pradhan, visits the house and takes to cheering up his mute daughter Hema.
who_initiates: Raju, through attention and music rather than declaration
courtship_pattern: Almost wordless on her side. He plays the dafli, she dances, and the relationship is conducted through music and protection rather than through speech or conventional courtship.
emotional_dynamic: Tender and protective, with a marked imbalance of power that the film treats as devotion rather than as control.
pair_conflict: None; they are aligned against the stepmother from the start.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict arises between them at any point. The film's entire opposition is the stepmother Savitri and later the vengeful Prakash.
external_opposition_explanation: Savitri forbids Hema to dance, resents her talent in favour of her own daughter, and throws her out of the house on her father's death. Prakash, who holds a grudge against Raju, attacks him near the end.
lover_boy_explanation: Raju's whole purpose is Hema's welfare: he cheers her, takes her away when she is evicted, supports her and restores the dancing she was forbidden. It is devotion in the strongest sense, falling short of the top band only because the film is also a musical about her talent rather than purely about the romance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The relationship has to be carried almost entirely without the heroine's speech, which throws the weight onto the musical sequences; the film is named in the main article among those that fixed Kapoor's romantic-star image.
actor_transformation: From a cheerful visitor to the person her survival depends on.
female_transformation: From a girl forbidden to dance and evicted from her home to one restored to both her art and her family.
relationship_outcome: Reunited, with the stepmother reconciled and accepting Hema as a daughter.
romantic_songs: 'Dafliwale Dafli Baja', 'Koyal Boli Duniya Doli', 'Parbat Ke Peechhe'
relationship_analysis: A romance of protection rather than pursuit, and the clearest case in the batch of the Kapoor hero as a woman's advocate against her own family. Mutuality and female agency sit below the film's warmth because Hema is largely acted upon, by her stepmother, by Raju and by the plot.
critical_reading: The film's treatment of a mute heroine is sympathetic and gives her a genuine talent to defend, but it also makes her wholly dependent on a man to voice and rescue her. The framing is protective in a way that reads as benevolent in 1979 and more constraining now.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the wealthy woman he sets out to win
how_they_meet: Not documented in detail; Ajay, a mechanic leading a double life as a conman, sets his sights on the wealthy Sheetal Khanna.
who_initiates: Ajay, as part of his ambition to marry money
courtship_pattern: Conducted under a false self throughout, by a man the film describes as a lying conman and Casanova, and complicated by his own brother competing for the same woman under another name.
emotional_dynamic: Built on invention, and undermined by the fact that nothing he says about himself is reliable.
pair_conflict: His lying, which is also what allows him to be framed for murder.
pair_friction_explanation: The relationship's problem is his own unreliability rather than any hostility between them. When the frame-up comes, his established dishonesty leaves him with no credible defence, which damages the relationship structurally.
external_opposition_explanation: Vikram, who is secretly Ajay's brother, works for Sheetal and hopes to marry her himself, and he and Prem conspire to frame Ajay for Mala's murder when they learn she might marry him.
lover_boy_explanation: The romantic pursuit is constant but mercenary in origin: he dreams of making it big with a wealthy woman. Kapoor plays the charm at full strength, and the film is explicit that it is a performance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The comedy depends on the established Kapoor and Neetu Singh rapport being used for a courtship the audience knows to be fraudulent.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the article's plot ends at the framing.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article stops once Vikram and Prem move against him.
relationship_analysis: A second instance in three years, after Rafoo Chakkar and Hum Kisise Kum Naheen, of a Kapoor courtship conducted under a false identity, here without the earlier films' excuse of self-protection. The cast list complicates the identity structure further by crediting Neetu Singh as Anita Verma / Sheetal Khanna while a separate actress is also credited as Anita Verma.
critical_reading: The film treats habitual lying as a comic trait and its consequence, an unprovable innocence, as the punishment, which is a neat moral structure. What it never addresses is that the woman is courted throughout by someone who does not exist.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: At college, where Vishal, believing himself wealthy, meets Neeta, the only daughter of the rich widower Gulabchand.
courtship_pattern: Brief and conventional, reaching a settled engagement early: Gulabchand and Vishal's brother Karan meet and finalise the marriage before the plot turns.
emotional_dynamic: Untroubled while it lasts, then suspended by catastrophe.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement is recorded. The relationship is disrupted by the murder of her father, the crippling of his brother and the discovery that Karan's life was a fiction, none of which involves the couple quarrelling.
external_opposition_explanation: Neeta's father is murdered and Vishal's brother is revealed as a circus trapeze artist and a suspect in that murder and a robbery, which places the engagement in an impossible position.
lover_boy_explanation: A conventional romantic lead in a film that turns into a crime drama about a brother's concealed life. The courtship is settled early and the second half belongs to the investigation.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Another of the many Kapoor and Neetu Singh pairings of the decade, with too little recorded here to distinguish it from the others.
actor_transformation: From a young man living on a comfortable fiction to one nursing a crippled brother and facing a police accusation.
female_transformation: Loses her father; the article does not follow her further.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with Inspector Yadav's revelation.
relationship_analysis: A slight romance in a film that reorganises itself around a brother's secret. Included because the engagement is a formal plot element with families on both sides, but the article gives the relationship no development after the disaster.
critical_reading: Neeta is defined by her father's wealth and then by his death, with no independent bearing on the plot. The film's interest is entirely in the two brothers.

initial_relationship: In love before the film's action
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article opens with the attachment established and the couple going to their fathers for consent.
who_initiates: Neither; the relationship is mutual from the outset
courtship_pattern: Skipped almost entirely. The film begins where most of Kapoor's romances end, with the request for permission, and spends its length on the marriage that follows the refusal.
emotional_dynamic: Steady and equal, tested by poverty and danger rather than by doubt.
pair_conflict: None; the couple is united throughout.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is recorded at any point. They elope together, work as driver and maid together, and face the employer's secret together.
external_opposition_explanation: Both fathers refuse and have other matches in mind; Bhagwant Singh advertises a reward for information on his daughter's whereabouts, which makes the marriage a fugitive one. A dangerous employer's secret then threatens their lives.
lover_boy_explanation: Chetan gives up his family and his standing to marry Payal and takes work as a driver to keep the marriage going. The devotion is complete and materially costly, falling short of the top band only because the film's second half turns on a thriller plot rather than on the romance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Their second film together after Zehreela Insaan, and the structure asks for partnership rather than charge, which suits the register both play.
actor_transformation: From a son seeking permission to a husband earning a living as a driver, with his wife in service beside him.
female_transformation: From a daughter under her father's authority to a woman working as a maid to keep her chosen marriage.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot ends with the couple in danger from their employer.
relationship_analysis: Structurally the most interesting romance of the batch after Badaltey Rishtey, because the marriage happens early and the film is about surviving it rather than achieving it. Mutuality scores at the top of the batch: both partners lose the same things and take equivalent work.
critical_reading: The film's sympathies are entirely with the couple against two equally obstinate fathers, and it is unusually willing to show what elopement actually costs in work and status. Payal's descent into domestic service is presented as shared hardship rather than as her disgrace, which reads well.

initial_relationship: Strangers; neighbours across a window
how_they_meet: Locked in his room after being expelled from college, Lucky meets Shanti through the window.
courtship_pattern: Comic and improvised: he steals Sujit Chopra's prize horse to impress her while working as a tangewala, and the courtship is a series of attempts to appear more than he is.
emotional_dynamic: Affectionate and light, with the pressure coming from her father's estimate of him rather than from anything between them.
pair_conflict: None directly; he withdraws himself under a promise to her father.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is recorded. The separation is self-imposed: he promises Shanti's father to keep away until he can find out who his real parents are.
external_opposition_explanation: Shanti's father Pukhraj disapproves of Lucky as ill-mannered and without familial background. The objection is specifically to his unknown parentage, which the discovery that he was found abandoned in a truck makes worse.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is energetic and drives several set pieces, and he accepts a painful condition to satisfy her father. But the film's second half turns on his adoption, his business and his fall into Sujit's orbit, and the romance recedes.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. One of the last of the run of Kapoor and Neetu Singh comedies that began in the mid-1970s, working on the familiar easy rapport rather than on anything specific to this film.
actor_transformation: The promise to her father sends him looking for his parentage, which begins the collapse into drink and Sujit's illegal business.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's summary breaks off at the revelation of his parents' identity.
relationship_analysis: A romance whose obstacle is parentage rather than money, which distinguishes it from the usual class-barrier plot: Shanti's father objects not to Lucky's poverty but to his having no known family at all. That objection is what sets the rest of the film in motion.
critical_reading: The demand that a man produce acceptable parents before he may court a woman is presented as a reasonable paternal concern, and Lucky accepts it without protest. Shanti herself is absent from the bargain struck over her.

initial_relationship: Employer's ward and tutor; she believes he is half of a married couple
how_they_meet: Ram and Rahim are hired as tutors to Sameera, the adopted daughter of two wealthy men, having assumed the identity of a married couple to get the position.
who_initiates: Both friends independently, which is the film's premise
courtship_pattern: Two friends courting the same woman from inside the same household and the same disguise, with the resolution left to her.
emotional_dynamic: A three-way affection in which the friendship is as much at stake as the romance.
pair_conflict: Not between Ram and Sameera; the conflict is between the two friends, and is handled by deferring to her.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing divides Ram and Sameera directly. The tension is the presence of Rahim and the false identity under which both men entered the house, so the friction is triangular rather than between the pair.
external_opposition_explanation: The false molestation charge engineered by Kundan is what drives them into the household under an assumed identity, and the standing obstacle thereafter is the rival claim of his closest friend.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is the film's business and Ram courts in earnest, but he shares the function equally with Rahim and the resolution is surrendered to Sameera rather than won. The role is romantic without being the film's sole romantic centre.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film's structure keeps the heroine's preference deliberately unresolved, so the playing has to hold two possible pairings open at once.
actor_transformation: From a disgraced student in disguise to one of two friends waiting on a woman's decision.
female_transformation: Moves from a ward being tutored to the person holding the film's only real decision.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article states that the choice is Sameera's and does not say how she chooses.
relationship_analysis: Notable for giving the heroine the deciding act, which is rare in this batch: the article's last word on the plot is that it is up to Sameera to choose her prospective life partner. Female agency is scored accordingly, even though almost nothing else about her is developed.
critical_reading: Both men enter her household under a false identity and court her from inside it, which the film treats as farce. Against that, the decision is genuinely hers and the friendship is never allowed to override her preference, which is more than most triangles of the period conceded.

actress_prominence: Female lead of the film's first chapter
initial_relationship: Teacher and pupil
how_they_meet: Mary arrives as a new teacher at the Christian school where Raju is the poorest boy and the class clown, and encourages him to find an ambition.
courtship_pattern: There is no courtship. A boy's first desire fixes on the one adult who is kind to him, expresses itself in a gift and a hidden drawing, and is never declared.
emotional_dynamic: Her warmth is teacherly and consistent; his is an overwhelming private longing she is not told about until it no longer matters.
pair_conflict: None between them. The obstacle is what he is: a schoolboy in love with a grown woman who is engaged.
pair_friction_explanation: Mary is never unkind and Raju never presses a claim. When she finds him at confession insisting he is not a child, she simply tells him a child cannot have sinned; the film locates the pain in the asymmetry rather than in any quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Mary has a companion, David, whom she marries; beyond that the barrier is structural, his age and her position as his teacher. David's suspicion, and his discovery of the paper with her picture ringed by a heart, is the only hostility directed at Raju, and even that ends with David handing the toy clown back.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is the whole content of Kapoor's segment and the boy's devotion is total, but there is no courtship, no rivalry he can enter and no possibility of requital. It is the lover-boy temperament before the lover-boy role, which is why the film reads retrospectively as the overture to Bobby.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The scenes require Kapoor to play unguarded adolescent longing against an adult who must remain kind without encouraging it, and the restraint on her side is what keeps the chapter from becoming uncomfortable.
actor_transformation: The loss is the beginning of the clown: he learns that the laughter he performs will have to cover his own grief, which is the film's whole thesis about him.
female_transformation: None; Mary marries David and leaves, and the film does not suggest the episode changed her.
relationship_outcome: Mary marries David with Raju standing as best man; David returns the toy clown to him as they drive away.
romantic_songs: 'Kehta Hai Joker Saara Zamana', 'Ae Bhai Zara Dekh Ke Chalo'
relationship_analysis: The earliest romance in the filmography and the only one in which Kapoor plays a child in love with an adult. It establishes the shape everything after it repeats in adult form: friction between the lovers at almost zero, the obstacle entirely outside the pair, and the man's identity organised around a woman who may not be available. Mutuality is the lowest score in the early work because the feeling runs one way only.
critical_reading: The film treats a boy's desire for his teacher with unusual frankness for 1970, including his glimpse of her undressing and the nude image he then confesses to, and it is careful to put the moral weight on his confusion rather than on her conduct. Read now, the sequence is still defensible precisely because Mary never reciprocates and the film never asks us to wish she would; what dates is the length of time it lingers on her body to establish his awakening.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Monty travels to Ooty on his doctors' advice to rest, and meets Tina, who lives there; the article records simply that they fall in love.
courtship_pattern: Quick and undramatised. The film is not interested in the courtship but in what Monty learns through Tina's household, which turns out to be the house his previous life was murdered for.
emotional_dynamic: Affectionate and largely untroubled, overtaken by the reincarnation plot as soon as it is established.
pair_conflict: None between them; the horror is that her guardian is his murderer.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Monty and Tina is recorded. What destabilises the relationship is external and concealed: the woman Tina calls Rani Sahiba is the Kamini who drove Ravi Verma off a cliff.
external_opposition_explanation: Kamini raised Tina, controls her, had her father killed by her own brother, and murdered Monty in his previous life. She is simultaneously the guardian standing between them and the target of the film's revenge.
lover_boy_explanation: Monty is a singer and a romantic figure and the courtship is genuine, but his governing drive is the recovery of a murdered life. The songs that define the role, above all 'Ek Hasina Thi', are instruments of memory and revenge rather than of courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film's charge is in the performance sequences rather than between the couple, and Tina functions largely as Monty's route into the Verma house.
actor_transformation: Not through the romance; Monty is changed by recovering Ravi's memory, and Tina is the occasion rather than the cause.
female_transformation: Learns that the woman who raised her had her father killed; the article does not follow the consequence.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot breaks off before the resolution.
romantic_songs: 'Dard-e-Dil', 'Om Shanti Om', 'Ek Hasina Thi'
relationship_analysis: A slight romance inside a reincarnation thriller, worth recording because Tina is the mechanism by which Monty reaches Kamini. The pairing marks the start of a run of four films with Tina Munim across 1980 to 1983, more than any actress other than Neetu Singh and Padmini Kolhapure in this stretch of the career.
critical_reading: Tina has no project of her own and exists to be loved and to be endangered by her guardian, which is standard for the genre. The film's real interest, a man avenging a murder committed against a body he no longer has, leaves the romance as decoration.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records that Sunny has fallen for Asha's younger sister Kim while the older generation's plot unfolds.
courtship_pattern: Undramatised. It runs as the youngest and lightest of the film's three romantic threads, beneath Johnny's and Vicky's claims on Asha.
emotional_dynamic: Uncomplicated young attachment, used for songs and relief rather than for conflict.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: The article records no disagreement. The couple is never the site of the film's conflict, which belongs to the lottery ticket and the fathers.
external_opposition_explanation: Kim and Asha are the daughters of Jaggi, the man Sunny's father Namdev is believed to have murdered, so the two families are joined by an unresolved killing. The conspirators who framed Namdev remain a live threat to both households.
lover_boy_explanation: A romantic supporting turn in a film whose weight is carried elsewhere. The courtship is sincere but Sunny neither pursues against opposition nor sacrifices anything for it; his function is to be the younger brother.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Kim Yashpal's role is small and the article gives the relationship in a single clause, leaving little to judge.
actor_transformation: None recorded.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Resolved with the family's reunion and the exposure of the conspirators.
romantic_songs: 'Chal Mere Bhai' is a brothers' number; the article does not identify romantic songs for this pairing.
relationship_analysis: The lightest of three parallel romances in a Manmohan Desai multi-starrer, and a clear illustration of how Kapoor's romantic function contracts when he is third-billed behind Amitabh Bachchan. It is recorded because the sisters' parentage ties the romance directly to the film's central crime.
critical_reading: Kim exists as the younger sister and the junior romantic pairing, with no independent stake in the lottery plot that defines both families. The film is not interested in her beyond the symmetry she provides.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is raising his dead brother's child
how_they_meet: Ravi, searching for the brother his father disowned, finds that Ramesh and Seema are dead and that Seema's sister Kanchan is raising their son; he meets her in the course of that search.
who_initiates: Both; the article records that they fall in love with each other
courtship_pattern: Begins in mutual ignorance of who he is and collapses the moment she learns, so the courtship runs forwards and then sharply into reverse.
emotional_dynamic: Genuinely mutual until her anger displaces it; thereafter she is defending herself against a repetition rather than responding to him.
pair_conflict: Kanchan refuses him outright on learning he is Nanda's son, certain she will be rejected for her poverty exactly as her sister was.
pair_friction_explanation: The rupture is between them and is hers: she is angry with Ravi and will have nothing to do with him. Its cause is external, his father's record, but the refusal itself is an interpersonal break rather than a barrier imposed on a united couple.
external_opposition_explanation: Nanda disinherited his elder son for marrying a poor woman and both that son and his wife are now dead. He is not opposing this match openly; he is pursuing the child by any means. The opposition operates as precedent, and it is powerful enough that the heroine enforces it herself.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi's activity in the film is almost entirely relational: finding his brother, reconciling his father, and then courting a woman who has good reason to refuse him. He persists against a refusal grounded in his own family's cruelty, which is the archetype's central move.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The first of six films with Padmini Kolhapure, and the relationship asks her to carry the film's moral position rather than merely be courted, which gives the pairing more friction than the usual Nasir Hussain romance.
actor_transformation: From a son who assumes his father can be talked round to a man courting against the documented consequences of his father's snobbery.
female_transformation: From a woman raising her sister's orphan to one refusing, on her sister's evidence, to repeat the marriage that destroyed her.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot ends with Nanda's plan to take the child by hook or by crook.
romantic_songs: 'Hoga Tumse Pyara Kaun', 'Poocho Na Yaar Kya Hua'
relationship_analysis: Structurally the most interesting romance of the early 1980s work because the external opposition is internalised by the heroine: Nanda never has to forbid this match, since Kanchan forbids it herself on the evidence of what he did to her sister. Female agency scores high for a Nasir Hussain musical for exactly that reason.
critical_reading: The film gives Kanchan a rational, evidence-based refusal and then requires the hero to overcome it, which means her judgement must ultimately be shown to be wrong. Read now, her position is the more defensible one, and the plot's demand that she set it aside is the weaker half of the film.

actress_prominence: Female lead, played by two actresses before and after reconstructive surgery
initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Vikram meets the singer Sunita while holidaying in Srinagar, and at the temple where they first meet the two vow never to part.
courtship_pattern: A rapid, song-driven courtship sealed by a temple vow, then a decade-long second courtship conducted by a man who does not know he is repeating himself.
emotional_dynamic: Ardent and mutual, then sustained on his side by mourning and on hers by a silence she is manipulated into keeping.
pair_conflict: None of their own making. Every division is manufactured by his mother.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple never quarrels. Such friction as the second half contains, her anger at his songs about love and her flight when he recognises her, comes from the lies she has been told, not from anything between them.
external_opposition_explanation: Sharda opposes the marriage because Sunita is penniless, and after the crash she tells Sunita that Vikram could never love her disfigured and tells Vikram that Sunita is dead. She refuses to reunite them even when Dr. Mehra begs her. The car crash, the coma and the disfigurement supply the rest.
lover_boy_explanation: Among the purest lover-boy constructions in the filmography. Vikram's entire adult life is organised around a vow to a woman he believes dead: he performs on stage to raise money for an orphanage in her memory, and recognises her finally by her mannerisms rather than her face. Devotion is the character's only content.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The premise splits the relationship across two actresses and asks Kapoor to play the same love twice without recognition, which works better in the songs than in the recognition scenes; Jaya Bachchan supplies Sunita's singing voice, adding a third performer to one character.
actor_transformation: From an ardent young lover to a man in permanent mourning who keeps a vow to a ghost, and finally to one who trusts a recognition everyone has told him is impossible.
female_transformation: From a penniless singer to a disfigured woman told she is unlovable, then to a surgically remade Kusum Mehra building a second life on a lie she did not choose.
relationship_outcome: Reunited at the temple where they first exchanged vows, and the promises are renewed.
romantic_songs: 'Yeh Vaada Raha', 'Tu Tu Hai Wahi', 'Mera Pyar Tera Pyar'
relationship_analysis: The clearest case in the filmography of a romance broken and sustained entirely from outside the couple: pair friction at three against external opposition at nine. One pairing row is used rather than two, because Poonam Dhillon and Tina Munim play one continuous character and one continuous relationship. The article records this as the first Hindi film to split a female lead between two actresses.
critical_reading: The film's engine is a mother persuading a disfigured woman that she is no longer lovable, and it is candid that this is a cruelty rather than a kindness. What it never questions is the remedy: Sunita becomes acceptable again only after surgery makes her beautiful, so the resolution quietly endorses the premise Sharda used against her.

initial_relationship: Childhood friends across an absolute class barrier
how_they_meet: They grew up together in the village, he the penniless orphan nephew of the priest and she the niece of the Bade Thakur, whose charity paid for his education in the city; he returns eight years later to find her grown.
who_initiates: Devdhar, and then only inwardly; he never declares himself while she is marriageable
courtship_pattern: There is no courtship in the first half at all. He intends to ask for her hand, meets the prince she is infatuated with, and says nothing. The relationship becomes real only after she is widowed and violated, and is then conducted as care rather than as wooing.
emotional_dynamic: One-sided and silent, then protective, and finally mutual on ground neither would have chosen.
pair_conflict: She does not reciprocate at first and is infatuated with another man; after her widowhood the difficulty is her own shame rather than any quarrel.
pair_friction_explanation: Dev never presses and Rama never rejects him unkindly; the early asymmetry is unspoken and the later relationship is unopposed between them. The friction belongs to her condition, not to the pair.
external_opposition_explanation: The whole social order stands against it: she is an aristocrat and he has no standing; she is being prepared to have her head shaved as a widow; she is raped by her own brother-in-law, the Raja; and her father and that brother-in-law swear to kill Dev and force her back to her marital home. The film ends in open violence in the village.
lover_boy_explanation: Devotion at its most costly. Dev's declared purpose is to rebuild Manorama's life and restore her faith in living, and he pursues it against custom, caste and armed men who intend to kill him. He courts a widow in a society that forbids it, which is rebellion for love in the strongest sense the period allowed.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film asks the two to play tenderness without courtship for most of its length, and the weight of Kapoor's performance sits in restraint rather than ardour; it is among the most substantial acting the filmography offers him.
actor_transformation: From a man who swallows his love out of gratitude to his patrons into one who confronts the entire order those patrons represent.
female_transformation: From an aristocratic girl infatuated with a prince to a widow stripped of everything, raped by her husband's brother, and then rebuilt into a woman who will accept a second life.
relationship_outcome: The article records that the young people are reunited after the fight in the village.
romantic_songs: 'Meri Kismat Mein Tu Nahin Shayad', 'Bhavre Ne Khilaya Phool', 'Yeh Galiyan Yeh Chaubara'
relationship_analysis: The most important romance in the filmography after Bobby and Laila Majnu, and the one that puts the lover-boy persona to the most serious use. The pattern is the same as in the 1970s films, friction near zero and opposition at maximum, but here the opposition is an explicit social prohibition rather than a father's preference, so the persona is made to carry an argument. Set against Ek Chadar Maili Si four years later, in which Kapoor plays a man who abuses the widow he is made to marry, it shows the full range the period allowed him.
critical_reading: The film is genuinely progressive in its subject, taking the side of widow remarriage against custom and refusing to treat Rama's violation as her disgrace. It is less comfortable in its method: the rape is a plot device that clears the way for the hero's project, and Rama's recovery is largely something done for her rather than by her. The film gives her the confession scene with her mother and little else of her own.

initial_relationship: Strangers in Lucknow's nawabi society
how_they_meet: Javed loves Firdous from a distance and hands his love letter to a man who turns out to be her brother Sikander; warned off, he enters the house disguised as a servant, and she recognises him as he leaves.
courtship_pattern: Conducted by trespass and by exchanged photographs: he infiltrates her household as a servant, takes her picture, and she comes to his house to retrieve it, at which point the attachment becomes mutual.
emotional_dynamic: Ardent and reciprocated, then suspended while two friends who love the same woman try to be generous to each other.
pair_conflict: Nothing between them; the obstruction is her father's verdict and then Akhtar's claim.
pair_friction_explanation: Javed and Firdous are never at odds. The relationship is interrupted by her father's refusal on grounds of family and then by the marriage Akhtar contracts on Javed's behalf, neither of which divides the couple from each other.
external_opposition_explanation: Her brother warns him off, and Nawab Mirza Changezi tells Javed outright that he cannot marry Firdous because of his family. Akhtar then marries her, intending to divorce her so Javed can have her, and on discovering she is his own beloved refuses to let her go.
lover_boy_explanation: Javed's entire function is to love Firdous and to keep trying: the letter, the disguise, the photograph, the decision to marry her against her father. What holds the score below the top band is that the film's resolution is taken out of his hands entirely and placed in Akhtar's.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, and the article notes the film was a box-office failure. The nawabi setting asks for a courtly register the plot keeps interrupting, and the triangle gives Jeetendra's Akhtar the more active half of the story.
actor_transformation: From a confident suitor to a man whose friend's act of generosity has become the obstacle in his way.
female_transformation: Married to one man in order to be given to another, without being consulted by either.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot ends on open questions about whether Javed gets Firdous and whether Akhtar will divorce her.
romantic_songs: 'Meri Zindagi Mein Aaye', 'Deedar-E-Yaar'
relationship_analysis: A period triangle in which the two men's friendship, not the woman's preference, organises the plot. The device, marrying a woman in order to divorce her and hand her on, is unusual even for the era and produces the film's one genuinely dramatic reversal.
critical_reading: Firdous is contracted, married and withheld entirely between men who both claim to love her, and the article's account gives her no voice in any of it; the film's closing questions are all about what the men will do. Female agency is the lowest score in this batch for that reason.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she believes him to be her dead sister's husband
how_they_meet: Rashmi returns home to find that her father has installed a man he believes to be Vijay, her lost sister's husband, as head of the business and heir to the estate.
who_initiates: Rashmi, who moves from suspicion to attachment
courtship_pattern: Inverted: she begins apprehensive of him and warms, so the courtship is her revision of an accurate first instinct rather than his pursuit.
emotional_dynamic: Wary, then affectionate on her side; on his, an attachment he can only keep by maintaining a fraud.
pair_conflict: He is not who she thinks he is, and the woman whose husband he claims to be is still alive.
pair_friction_explanation: Her initial apprehension is real but short-lived, and there is no open quarrel. The corrosive element is the deception itself, which the article leaves unexposed when the plot breaks off.
