external_opposition_explanation: Dr. Joshi knows he is an ex-convict jailed for theft and wanted for murder, and arrives with the amnesiac Juhi, the real Vijay's wife. Both threaten to collapse the identity the relationship rests on.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is central to the plot and he does come to want it genuinely, but the character's organising activity is holding a stolen identity. Courtship is something that happens to him inside the imposture rather than the reason for it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The seventh and last of the Kapoor and Tina Munim films, and the premise requires him to be charming while the audience knows he is a fraud, which is the register he had already used in Jhoota Kahin Ka.
actor_transformation: From an impostor exploiting a family's grief to a man with something real to lose by being found out.
female_transformation: From a woman rightly suspicious of a stranger in her father's house to one in love with him.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with Dr. Joshi's arrival and the threat of exposure.
relationship_analysis: Notable as a gender inversion of Kati Patang, where a woman assumes a dead person's identity in a grieving household; here Kapoor takes that position and the romance is built on the fraud. It is the third film in the batch, after Jhoota Kahin Ka and Rafoo Chakkar, in which he courts under a false name.
critical_reading: Rashmi's instinct about him is correct and the plot requires her to abandon it, which is the same structure as Zamaane Ko Dikhana Hai: a woman's accurate judgement treated as an obstacle to be overcome. The film shows no interest in what the deception costs her.

initial_relationship: Strangers, though both were attached to the same household as children
how_they_meet: Ravi meets Roma by a turn of circumstances and saves Mohan Kumar's life in the process; neither knows that she was the ward of his own family and he the son of the man wrongly imprisoned for her father's murder.
who_initiates: Not documented; the article records that they fall in love
courtship_pattern: Undramatised and overtaken by the revenge plot; the relationship's function is to bring two dispersed halves of the same wrecked household back into the same room.
emotional_dynamic: Straightforward attachment between two people the plot has orphaned in different ways.
pair_conflict: None between them; he is working for the men who destroyed her father and his.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Ravi and Roma is recorded. The tension is that Ravi is in the employ of Jugal Kishore, who murdered her father and framed his, a fact neither of them knows.
external_opposition_explanation: Jugal Kishore and his partners murdered Roma's father, framed Ravi's, and finally kidnap both Ravi and Roma to extort a ransom once they learn whose son he is. She also lives under the guardianship of a mean, alcoholic uncle.
lover_boy_explanation: Third-billed behind Ashok Kumar and Dilip Kumar, Kapoor plays a gangster's man discovering his parentage. The romance is real but the role's weight is the father-and-son recognition, and there is no courtship, rebellion or sacrifice for love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Amrita Singh's Roma is a plot connector as much as a romantic lead, and the article's account gives the relationship a sentence.
actor_transformation: Not through the romance; he is changed by discovering that the man he was sent to kill is his father.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond being kidnapped and recovered.
relationship_outcome: Both are rescued when Mohan Kumar and Ravi collaborate to kill Jugal Kishore.
relationship_analysis: A romance that doubles as a second family reunion the characters cannot see: Roma was raised close to the household Ravi was lost from. It is recorded because it is the point at which the film's scattered survivors are brought back together, not because the relationship itself is developed.
critical_reading: Roma is defined by the men around her, a murdered father, an abusive uncle, a lover in a gang, and the film's interest in her stops at her usefulness to the recognition plot.

initial_relationship: Neighbours
how_they_meet: Salim relocates to Lucknow for work and meets Salma, his attractive neighbour; the article records that both fall in love.
courtship_pattern: A neighbourly attachment that never gets the chance to become a courtship: her father confines her to the house, then sells it and takes her out of the country.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and unforced, ended by force before it can develop.
pair_conflict: None between them at any point.
pair_friction_explanation: Salim and Salma are never in conflict. The relationship is destroyed entirely from outside, and his later degradation is grief rather than any quarrel with her.
external_opposition_explanation: Her widower father Hamid promised her mother that Salma would marry the wealthy Anwar. He forbids her to leave the house, and when she persists he sells the house and relocates the family to Lahore, in another country. Salim tries to stop them and is assaulted senseless. The separation is absolute and permanent.
lover_boy_explanation: Salim is a poet as well as an architect and the role is built on romantic devotion and its collapse: he attempts to physically stop her removal, is beaten for it, and never gives up hope of reunion even inside another marriage. The register is ruin rather than triumph, which is where it differs from Bobby.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The third of six Kapoor and Padmini Kolhapure films, and the relationship is more sketched than played, since the plot removes her early and keeps her offstage.
actor_transformation: The loss turns an architect and poet into a drunk who frequents a brothel, and he never stops expecting to recover her.
female_transformation: Confined, then removed across a national border to be married to a man chosen before she was born.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with Salim still hoping for reunion while trapped in his marriage to Sahira.
relationship_analysis: The most extreme external opposition in the batch: a father who liquidates his property and emigrates to end a courtship. It is one of very few Kapoor romances broken by the partition of the subcontinent rather than by a family's preference alone, which makes the obstacle political as well as domestic.
critical_reading: The promise Hamid made to his dying wife is treated by the film as a real claim on him, which gives the opposition more dignity than usual. Salma herself is given one act of resistance, persisting after being confined, and is then removed from the film; the consequences are dramatised entirely through Salim's decline.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the new neighbour's daughter
how_they_meet: Salim's mother, alarmed by his drinking and his visits to the courtesan Phoolrani, compels him to marry the daughter of their new neighbours.
who_initiates: Neither; his mother arranges it and he consents reluctantly
courtship_pattern: None. The marriage precedes any acquaintance and he continues visiting the brothel afterwards, so there is no courtship at any stage.
emotional_dynamic: A wife trying to hold a husband who is openly waiting for another woman.
pair_conflict: He does not love her, is frequently absent at a brothel, and hopes to be reunited with Salma; she will not let him go.
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is substantial and mutual in effect if not in intent: his neglect and continued visits to Phoolrani on one side, and on the other a wife the article describes as seemingly demure but unwilling to release him. This is conflict inside the couple, not opposition from outside.
external_opposition_explanation: His mother arranged the marriage over his objection, which is the reason the relationship exists at all. Beyond that there is no external force acting on it.
lover_boy_explanation: In this relationship Kapoor plays an absent and unwilling husband whose attention is directed at another woman and a brothel. There is no courtship, no devotion and no sacrifice; the lover-boy apparatus is pointed away from his wife.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The part gives Deepti Naval the film's late reversal, a wife who turns out to be less yielding than she appeared, and the article's account rests on that turn rather than on any rapport.
actor_transformation: None; he remains oriented towards Salma throughout, which is the marriage's problem.
female_transformation: From a demure arranged bride to a woman asserting a claim on a husband who wants to leave.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with Sahira refusing to let him go easily.
relationship_analysis: The second of two relationships in one film, and the counterweight to the Salma thread: one romance destroyed by a father, one marriage imposed by a mother. Taken together they make this the clearest early instance of Kapoor playing a man whose romantic life is entirely arranged by other people's parents.
critical_reading: The film frames Sahira's refusal to release her husband as an unwelcome surprise, the sting in the tail of his predicament, which puts the audience with the neglectful husband rather than the wife he married under duress and then abandoned nightly. Read now she has the stronger case, and the film's sympathies are misallocated.

initial_relationship: Not documented
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records only that the two brothers fall in love with the same woman.
courtship_pattern: Not documented. The relationship is stated rather than shown in the article's five-sentence summary.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented.
pair_conflict: His brother is his rival, and he is a criminal while his brother is a police inspector.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Ravi and Sheetal is recorded; the rivalry is between the brothers. Scored low and provisionally, since the article gives the relationship a single clause.
external_opposition_explanation: His own brother is the competing claim, and Ravi's work for the don J. D. places him on the wrong side of the law from the family he is estranged from.
lover_boy_explanation: A conventional second-lead romance in a film about two estranged brothers and a murdered father. The courtship is asserted rather than dramatised and nothing in the role is organised around it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, and the article documents almost none of the relationship. There is not enough recorded interaction to judge it.
actor_transformation: Persuaded to leave the criminal world, though the article attributes this to the brothers' reconciliation rather than to the romance.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article does not say which brother ends with her.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the article explicitly makes the shared attachment one of the causes of the brothers' estrangement, but scored thinly: the summary states the triangle in one clause and resolves it in another without naming an outcome.
critical_reading: Too little survives to read the film's framing. Sheetal is the object over which two brothers are divided and then reconciled, and the article does not record a preference of her own.

initial_relationship: Acquainted; she works at a hotel he brings tourists to
how_they_meet: Amar works as a guide in Kashmir and is in love with Bhavna, a hotel receptionist, but is too afraid to tell her; her sister Sangeeta engineers the declaration.
who_initiates: Amar, with Sangeeta's help, after being unable to speak for himself
courtship_pattern: Almost entirely pre-verbal: a long unspoken attachment, a single brokered declaration, and then a death before any marriage can be arranged.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and delighted for a very short stretch, then a devotion that survives only as her derangement.
pair_conflict: None whatever.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no conflict between Amar and Bhavna. His shyness delays the relationship and her sister resolves it; from the declaration to his fall the pair is entirely united.
external_opposition_explanation: Amar falls from a mountain to his apparent death before any marriage can be settled. Bhavna later maintains the fall was a homicide rather than an accident, and Vikram Mehra, whom Amar had violently warned away from Sangeeta, is the standing suspicion.
lover_boy_explanation: Amar is a pure romantic lead in the Kashmiri-guide mould, with the relationship as his only project, and the film kills him at the peak of it. The score sits below the top band because the character's defining trait is an inability to declare himself, and because the second half belongs to his double.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Shabana Azmi is cast against the usual register of a Kapoor romance and carries most of the film's aftermath; the courtship itself is brief and played lightly before the tonal break.
actor_transformation: From a man who cannot speak to a man who has spoken and is immediately killed for the film's purposes; the arc is cut off rather than completed.
female_transformation: From a hotel receptionist in love to a woman who loses her mind at his death, is treated by having a stranger impersonate him, and then fights to prove he was murdered.
relationship_outcome: Ended by Amar's apparent death; Bhavna recovers slowly through a deception rather than through reunion.
relationship_analysis: The first of two romances in a double-role film, and the one that produces the premise: Amar's death is what makes his double's impersonation necessary. It is worth recording that the grieving woman is given the investigative drive here, which is unusual, and that the article ends on whether anyone will believe her.
critical_reading: The film's treatment of Bhavna's breakdown is instrumental: her madness exists so that a lookalike can be brought in to treat it, and her insistence that the death was murder is framed as the possibly unreliable claim of someone who has lost her mind. That framing is the most troubling thing in the film, and it is also the source of its interest.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the sister of the woman his double loved
how_they_meet: Flight Lieutenant Pawan Kumar Saxena comes to Kashmir on a visit and is immediately mistaken for the dead Amar; Sangeeta approaches him because Dr. Mehra needs him to impersonate her sister's lover.
who_initiates: Sangeeta, who sets out to seduce him into agreeing
courtship_pattern: Begins as a deliberate seduction undertaken for someone else's benefit and turns into a real attachment, so the sequence runs from instrumentality to feeling rather than the reverse.
emotional_dynamic: Calculated on her side at the outset and genuine on his; the article records that he is really in love with her.
pair_conflict: She approaches him as a means to her sister's recovery, and he is required to spend the relationship pretending to be another man.
pair_friction_explanation: Pawan refuses the impersonation and has to be seduced into it, which is a real disagreement resolved by manipulation rather than persuasion. Once he agrees the pair is not in open conflict, but the relationship is founded on her using him.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is Bhavna's condition and the therapeutic fiction built around it: Pawan can only be with Sangeeta while maintaining the pretence of being her sister's dead lover, and Bhavna's discovery that he loves Sangeeta is what turns her towards proving the murder.
lover_boy_explanation: Pawan is not courting; he is recruited, seduced and then conscripted into wearing a dead man's face. The romance happens to him in the middle of someone else's treatment plan, and the role has none of the archetype's initiative.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The article notes that Kapoor took seven slaps from Padmini Kolhapure in a single scene, which suggests the register between them was combative rather than tender; this is the fifth of their six films together.
actor_transformation: From a stranger who refuses to impersonate a dead man to one doing it daily for the sake of the woman who talked him into it.
female_transformation: From a sister who will use her own body to secure her sister's recovery to a woman genuinely attached to the man she recruited.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot ends with Bhavna's attempt to prove the death was murder.
relationship_analysis: The second romance in the same film and the inverse of the first: where Amar and Bhavna are frictionless and doomed, Pawan and Sangeeta begin in manipulation and survive. Female agency is scored at eight, the highest in the batch, because Sangeeta drives the entire second half, though what she drives is a deception.
critical_reading: The film treats a woman seducing a man in order to install him as her sister's therapy as an act of familial devotion, and never asks what is owed to the man being used or to the patient being deceived. It is the most ethically careless premise in the batch, and the film's own framing is entirely untroubled by it.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he is newly arrived in her town
how_they_meet: Ravi moves to Goa from the United States, into the neighbourhood where Mona runs a small restaurant and where Raja, her close friend, has loved her for years without saying so.
who_initiates: Mutual; the article records that Mona and Ravi fall in love
courtship_pattern: An open, uncomplicated courtship conducted in full view of the one person it destroys, since Raja knows nothing of it until it is settled.
emotional_dynamic: Warm, mutual and unguarded, and unknowingly cruel to the third party.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: Ravi and Mona are never divided. The film's pain is located in Raja, who loves her and cannot say so, and in the grandmother's objection; the couple itself is stable throughout.
external_opposition_explanation: Ravi's grandmother Kamladevi opposes the match on grounds of class difference: he belongs to a rich industrialist family and Mona runs a small restaurant among fishermen. Raja's unspoken prior claim is the other standing obstacle, and it is removed only by his death.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi is a straightforward romantic hero in a film built entirely on love, and he holds to Mona against his own family. What keeps the score out of the top band is that he neither knows about nor resolves the film's central conflict: the decisive act of love in Saagar is Raja's, not his.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing directly. The casting is the point: Kapoor and Dimple Kapadia reunited twelve years after Bobby, she in her comeback, and the film trades openly on the audience's memory of the earlier pairing. The ease between them is the strongest thing in the film after Kamal Haasan's performance.
actor_transformation: Little of his own; he arrives in love with her and ends married to her, and the change the film dramatises belongs to Raja.
female_transformation: From a woman running a restaurant with a friend she does not know loves her to a wife who has cost that friend his life.
relationship_outcome: They marry, after Raja sacrifices both his love and his life for them.
romantic_songs: 'Sach Mere Yaar Hai', 'Yun Hi Gaate Raho', 'Jaane Do Na'
relationship_analysis: The most important pairing of the mid-1980s work, and the one deliberately built on the audience's memory of Bobby twelve years earlier. Structurally it inverts the usual arrangement: the Kapoor character is the one who gets the girl easily, while the romantic suffering, the devotion and the sacrifice, everything the lover-boy archetype normally supplies, is given to Kamal Haasan.
critical_reading: The film is unusually clear-eyed that the successful romance is also an injury to someone else, and it refuses to make Raja a rival to be defeated. Mona is given real work, a business and a choice, and the class objection comes from Ravi's family rather than hers, which reverses the Bobby arrangement. What the film cannot quite manage is why she chooses as she does, since Ravi is the less interesting of the two men.

initial_relationship: Strangers forced to share a house at knifepoint
how_they_meet: The mafia lord Rahim Shaikh pushes into Dawood's room with a bejewelled woman and tells him to let her stay the night or be killed; by morning the neighbourhood has decided she is his wife and arranged a feast for the couple.
who_initiates: Neither; the cohabitation is imposed and the feeling grows out of it
courtship_pattern: Marriage first and courtship never: they live as a pretend married couple under the neighbourhood's eye, and the attachment accumulates through her conduct in the household rather than through any wooing.
emotional_dynamic: His resentment against her steadiness, slowly converting into respect and then into love he is the last to recognise.
pair_conflict: He is angry at being saddled with her and is courting another woman throughout; she is another man's property and expects to be reclaimed.
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is real and one-directional: Dawood is angry with Sultana for the position she has put him in, and is pursuing Kaynat while Sultana keeps his house. It is resentment rather than hostility, and it dissolves as he comes to see what she is doing.
external_opposition_explanation: Sultana was purchased by Rahim Shaikh to be resold to the highest bidder, and his men warn both of them to stay together only until he is released to claim her. Her standing as a courtesan is the other barrier: it is why Kaynat's family can be told about a first wife and why the relationship is socially impossible.
lover_boy_explanation: The role turns on a man choosing a courtesan against his own prospects and the neighbourhood's expectations, and ends with him going to take her back from the man who owns her. The devotion is genuine but arrives very late, and for most of the film his romantic attention is directed at Kaynat instead.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The relationship has to be built almost entirely out of domestic detail rather than romantic scenes, since the couple are pretending to be married while he courts someone else, and the article's account gives Sultana the better of the material.
actor_transformation: From a man humiliated by a forced pretence into one who chooses the woman society has priced and discarded.
female_transformation: From a purchased woman waiting to be resold to one who sells her own jewels to feed his household, rescues a neighbour's girl from a trafficker, and leaves quietly rather than damage him.
relationship_outcome: Not documented in full; Dawood goes to rescue Sultana from Rahim Shaikh and the article's plot breaks off during the attempt.
relationship_analysis: The strongest female part in the batch and one of the few Kapoor romances in which the woman's actions, not the man's, accumulate the moral weight: every decisive gesture in the relationship is Sultana's. The structure also inverts the standard pattern, since the marriage is the premise and the love is the conclusion.
critical_reading: A B. R. Chopra social film that takes the standing of a courtesan as its subject and gives Sultana dignity, competence and initiative rather than pathos. Its limit is the usual one: her worth has to be demonstrated through service to a household and a rescue of another woman before the hero can be permitted to want her, and the film never questions that she must earn what Kaynat is granted by respectability.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he finds a manuscript she has lost
how_they_meet: Dawood finds a manuscript on a bus carrying the author's name and address, goes to return it, and meets Kaynat; he then introduces her to Sulaiman, the editor at his publishing house.
who_initiates: Mutual, after he has made her career possible
courtship_pattern: A literary courtship conducted through the publication of her novel, and consummated in a mutual declaration once the book is out.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and equal, and ended by her own decision rather than by any failure between them.
pair_conflict: She learns he already has a wife living in his house, which he has not explained.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple is not in conflict; the rupture is a single devastating discovery, and Kaynat goes to Sultana to establish the facts rather than quarrelling with him. Once she has them she acts.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is the pretend marriage the neighbourhood has already sanctioned: Kaynat's family is told there is a first wife, and the arrangement Rahim Shaikh forced on Dawood makes an honest proposal impossible.
lover_boy_explanation: Dawood courts Kaynat sincerely for most of the film and it is the relationship he intends to marry into, but he is also concealing a household, and the film ultimately has him redirect. The romantic energy is real and misdirected.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The relationship is written as the respectable alternative to Sultana and functions structurally, so the playing has less to work with than the central pairing.
actor_transformation: He is corrected rather than transformed: Kaynat tells him where his feeling actually lies and sends him to act on it.
female_transformation: From an unpublished writer to a published one, and from a woman expecting to marry him to the person who identifies the marriage he should make instead.
relationship_outcome: Kaynat relinquishes him, makes him realise he loves Sultana, and encourages him to bring her back.
relationship_analysis: The second relationship in the same film and the one that resolves the first. Female agency is scored at eight because Kaynat performs the film's decisive act: she establishes the truth from Sultana directly, reaches her own judgement, and redirects the hero against her own interest.
critical_reading: The film gives Kaynat a profession, a public success and the moral intelligence to settle the plot, which is more than the respectable second heroine usually receives. The renunciation is still a renunciation, and the structure requires one woman to stand aside so the other can be rewarded.

initial_relationship: Strangers married by their fathers' arrangement
how_they_meet: They do not meet before the wedding. Kishan's father Bhim and Chando's father Ramlal are close friends, and Bhim arranges the marriage without his son's consent to relieve his friend's difficulty in finding her a groom.
who_initiates: Neither; both fathers arrange it and Kishan consents only out of fear
courtship_pattern: None, before or after. He refuses her the marriage entirely, will not sleep in the same bed, and leaves the city to be rid of her.
emotional_dynamic: Sustained revulsion on his side against uncomprehending devotion on hers; the article is explicit that she does not realise he hates her.
pair_conflict: He finds her ugly and graceless, will not live with her as a husband, marries another woman, and abandons her at a railway station.
pair_friction_explanation: This is sustained cruelty inside the marriage rather than any external obstacle: refusal of the marriage bed, concealment of her existence, bigamy, and abandonment at a station in a strange city. The article notes she continues serving her duties as a loyal wife throughout, which makes the friction entirely one-directional.
external_opposition_explanation: His father Bhim arranged the marriage without consent and later threatens him into taking Chando to Bombay, so the family that created the marriage also enforces it. There is no outside force opposing the couple; the family is the reason they are together at all.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is the flat negation of the archetype. Kishan's conduct towards his wife is contempt, concealment and abandonment; there is no courtship, no devotion and no sacrifice of any kind in this relationship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The part asks Radhika to play unreciprocated devotion without self-pity, and the article's summary gives her the film's sympathy throughout; Kapoor is required to be unlikeable for most of the running time.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the article's plot breaks off before any reckoning, with the two wives becoming friends in his house.
female_transformation: From an unwanted bride to a maid in her own husband's second household, keeping his secret and teaching his second wife how to be a wife.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with Chando installed as a servant and befriending Radha.
relationship_analysis: With Ek Chadar Maili Si in the same year, this is the clearest evidence that by the mid-1980s Kapoor was being cast in roles that invert the lover-boy persona rather than extend it. Pair friction at eight against external opposition at six reverses the signature pattern of the 1970s films entirely: here the husband is the obstacle.
critical_reading: The film's premise is that Chando's dark skin and plainness explain and partly excuse her husband's revulsion, and it stages her eventual acceptability through a makeover. That framing is the film's own and is recorded here rather than endorsed: on the article's account she is wronged continuously and her loyalty is treated as a virtue rather than as a symptom of having no alternative.

initial_relationship: Strangers; both are award-winners at the same ceremony
how_they_meet: Kishan meets Radha, an attractive woman from Bombay, when both are honoured at an awards ceremony for their work; after transferring to Bombay he ends up staying at her house.
courtship_pattern: A genuine courtship, conducted entirely on the concealment of an existing marriage, and completed in a bigamous wedding.
emotional_dynamic: Affectionate and mutual on its own terms, and false in its foundation.
pair_conflict: He never tells her he is already married, and installs his first wife in their house as a servant.
pair_friction_explanation: There is little open conflict between Kishan and Radha; the damage is the undisclosed marriage, which she does not learn of within the article's account. The friction is latent rather than expressed.
external_opposition_explanation: His father's enforcement of the first marriage is what brings Chando to Bombay, and Chando's presence in the house is the standing threat to this one. The obstacle is the marriage he concealed rather than any objection to Radha.
lover_boy_explanation: With Radha the role does deploy courtship and charm, and the attachment is the one he chose for himself. It cannot score higher because the whole relationship rests on a bigamy he maintains deliberately.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film uses Radha as the desirable alternative against which Chando is measured, so the pairing is written to be attractive rather than complex.
actor_transformation: None; the second marriage is the continuation of his evasion rather than a change in him.
female_transformation: Becomes close to the maid who is in fact her husband's first wife, and is taught by her how to be a traditional wife.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot breaks off with the two women becoming close and Radha receiving a makeover.
relationship_analysis: The second of two marriages in one film, and the one he chose. Recording both separately is what makes the film legible: the same man scores one on lover-boy with the wife imposed on him and five with the wife he selected, which is a useful demonstration that the archetype is a function of the role's construction rather than of the performer.
critical_reading: The film's sympathies are managed by contrast, and Radha's principal narrative function is to be what Chando is not. The most striking thing in the article's account is that the two women's friendship, not either marriage, becomes the relationship the plot is actually interested in.

initial_relationship: Brother-in-law and sister-in-law; he is her protector against her husband
how_they_meet: They are already living in the same village household when the film opens, Rano married to his drunken brother Trilok and Mangal the only member of the family who can shield her from him.
who_initiates: Neither; after Trilok's murder custom compels the marriage
courtship_pattern: None. The relationship converts from protection to marriage by the operation of custom, with no courtship at any point and no consent sought from either.
emotional_dynamic: Protective trust replaced by frustration and violence; the article records that he abuses her in his frustration as her first husband had.
pair_conflict: A marriage neither chose, to a man ten years her junior who had been her defender and becomes another source of harm.
pair_friction_explanation: The article is explicit that Mangal abuses Rano the same way Trilok did after marrying her. That is conflict and harm inside the couple, not opposition imposed on it, and it is the more devastating because he had been the one person protecting her.
external_opposition_explanation: The custom that requires a widow to marry her dead husband's brother is what creates the marriage. Around it sit a mother-in-law who berates Rano constantly over her dowry, a blind father-in-law who can do nothing, the murder of Trilok, and the rape of the girl that precipitated it.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is the furthest Kapoor travels from the lover-boy archetype in the whole filmography. Mangal does not court, does not choose and does not protect once he becomes a husband; what the part requires is resentment and violence.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The age difference is written into the premise, with Hema Malini playing a woman ten years the elder, and the discomfort of the pairing is the point rather than a flaw; the register is literary rather than romantic.
actor_transformation: A reversal rather than a development: from Rano's only defender to a husband who treats her as his brother did.
female_transformation: From a feisty woman enduring one bad marriage to a widow forced into a second with the boy who used to shield her.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's account ends with the marriage and his abuse of her.
romantic_songs: None; the film is not constructed around romantic songs.
relationship_analysis: The darkest pairing in the filmography and the most complete inversion of the persona: friction at eight, lover-boy at one, and a woman worse off at the end of the relationship than at its start. Read alongside Prem Rog four years earlier, in which Kapoor plays a man who defies a village to marry a widow honourably, it shows the two opposite things the same actor and the same social material could be made to do.
critical_reading: The film is adapted from a Sahitya Akademi-winning novella and does not pretend the karewa custom is benign: the marriage is presented as an imposition that damages both parties and destroys the one safe relationship Rano had. Its unsparing quality is its value. What the article's summary leaves unclear is whether the film offers Rano any resolution at all, and on the evidence available it does not.

actress_prominence: Supporting; named as his love interest
initial_relationship: Not documented
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records only that Raji, a gypsy girl, plays Mangal's love interest.
courtship_pattern: Not documented. The article gives the relationship a single clause and develops none of it.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented.
pair_conflict: Not documented; the pressure on it is the forced marriage to his brother's widow.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing between them is recorded. Scored low and provisionally: the obstacle to this attachment is the karewa marriage imposed on Mangal, not any conflict with Raji.
external_opposition_explanation: The custom compelling Mangal to marry Rano forecloses any other attachment, and Raji's status as a gypsy places her outside the village household entirely. The opposition is the same social machinery that produces the main marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: The attachment is named rather than dramatised, and the article gives Mangal no courtship, declaration or sacrifice for Raji. It registers chiefly as the thing the forced marriage costs him.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing and the article documents almost nothing of it. There is not enough recorded interaction to judge.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the article names Raji explicitly as Mangal's love interest, which makes her the woman he might have chosen against the widow he is given. That contrast is analytically useful even though the relationship itself is undocumented, and every score here is provisional.
critical_reading: Too little survives to read the film's framing beyond the structural point: the man's own attachment is a single clause while the marriage forced on him is the subject of the film.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is a pickpocket and one of Daaga's victims
how_they_meet: Not documented in detail; the article records that Prakash falls for a pickpocket, Shanti, who is a victim of Daaga.
courtship_pattern: Undramatised. It is the third and lightest of the film's three parallel romances, running beneath the friendship plot that organises everything.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented beyond the fact of his attachment.
pair_conflict: None between them; she is one of the gangster's victims, which ties her to the film's central antagonism.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is recorded. Their difference in standing, a criminal lawyer and a pickpocket, is not presented as a source of friction in the article's account.
external_opposition_explanation: Daaga is the source of the harm done to Shanti and the threat to all three friends throughout, and the film's resolution is his defeat rather than anything specific to this couple.
lover_boy_explanation: Third-billed in a film about three male friends, Prakash is a lawyer whose defining acts are professional and fraternal: defending Sandeep and fabricating a wife for him to secure the acquittal. The romance is a strand the plot does not pursue.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The article's plot is written in unusually compressed prose and states the relationship without showing it, leaving little to assess.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Resolved with the friends' reunion and Daaga's defeat.
relationship_analysis: A minor romance in a friendship film, recorded because the article names it directly. Its interest is that Kapoor's character is the one given a woman outside respectable society, which the plot then makes nothing of.
critical_reading: Shanti is identified by her offence and by her victimhood and is given nothing else; the film's attention belongs to the three men and the injury done to Ranjit's wife.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she has sought him out to kill him
how_they_meet: Rajiv returns from studying abroad and meets Rajni, an orphan without family or connections, and falls in love with her; she is an ichchhadhari naagin who came for him because the snake killed to revive him as a child was her husband.
who_initiates: Rajni, who arranged the meeting for a purpose Rajiv never learns of
courtship_pattern: A rapid courtship against his mother's preference, followed by a marriage the couple are shown enjoying; the film spends its length not on winning her but on keeping them both alive.
emotional_dynamic: Genuinely affectionate and, on her side, in unresolved contradiction with the revenge she arrived to carry out.
pair_conflict: She married him intending to kill him, and abandons that purpose without ever telling him.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no quarrel between them and Rajiv is never aware of any threat. The friction is a concealed lethal intent she chooses not to act on, which is real but entirely one-sided and unspoken.
external_opposition_explanation: Thakur Ajay Singh has managed the estate for years expecting his daughter to marry Rajiv, and sends men to kill Rajni and later attacks Rajiv himself. Bhairo Nath, the snake-charming tantric, identifies her and sends a serpent to kill Rajiv in hospital. Rajiv's mother initially refuses her blessing because Rajni is an orphan without connections.
lover_boy_explanation: Rajiv marries against his mother's wishes and the Thakur's plans, which is genuine romantic defiance, but for most of the film he is the protected party rather than the agent: he is unconscious, attacked, or unaware while his wife fights for him. The role has the archetype's position without its initiative.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film is remembered for Sridevi rather than for the couple, and the pairing works because Kapoor plays the ordinary man convincingly enough to make her transformation the spectacle; his ordinariness is the role's function.
actor_transformation: Very little, and deliberately so; Rajiv ends the film as he began it, and never learns what his wife is or what she gave up for him.
female_transformation: From a widow who came to avenge her husband to one who kills her own ally to save the man she was sent to destroy.
relationship_outcome: Rajni fights off the serpents sent to kill Rajiv and destroys Bhairo Nath, choosing the marriage over the vengeance she came for.
romantic_songs: 'Main Teri Dushman', 'Balma', 'Tune O Rangeele'
relationship_analysis: Female agency at nine is the highest score in the batch and one of the highest in the filmography, because every consequential act in the relationship is Rajni's: the meeting, the marriage, the concealment, the defence and the renunciation. It is a useful corrective to the assumption that the Kapoor romantic hero is always the mover; here the heroine has supernatural power and he has none.
critical_reading: The film's own framing makes the wife's power the source of both the danger and the salvation, and it resolves by having her give up a legitimate claim of vengeance for a husband who does not know he was ever at risk. That she is never permitted to tell him, and that her sacrifice is invisible to its beneficiary, is the most interesting thing about the pairing and the thing the film is least interested in examining.

initial_relationship: Married; the marriage is established when the film opens
how_they_meet: They do not meet in the film. Ram and Sita are already married and living in the Dhanraj joint household when the story begins.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The film is about the destruction of an existing marriage rather than the making of one.
emotional_dynamic: A working marriage poisoned from outside and then from within, with her closeness to his younger brother read by him as proof of an affair.
pair_conflict: He believes she is sleeping with his brother Amar, and goes on believing it after Amar marries someone else and after she becomes pregnant with his own child.
pair_friction_explanation: The damage is entirely internal to the couple and entirely his: he spies on his wife, sustains the suspicion against every piece of contrary evidence, assumes her pregnancy is his brother's, and courts another woman. Sita gives him no cause at any point, which makes this friction rather than opposition.
external_opposition_explanation: His sister Uma plants the suggestion deliberately in order to set him against Sita, and the household is run by a mother who is violent towards her daughters-in-law. The secrecy Amar and Sita maintain, which Ram misreads, exists only because that mother would make trouble about Amar's own romance.
lover_boy_explanation: In this relationship Kapoor plays a jealous husband rather than a lover: there is no courtship, no devotion and no sacrifice, and his romantic energy is redirected to another woman while his wife carries his child. The role is a deliberate inversion of the persona.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The part requires Kapoor to be steadily unsympathetic against a wife the film keeps entirely blameless, and the article's summary gives Jaya Prada's Sita the moral position throughout.
actor_transformation: A deterioration rather than an arc: from husband to spy, to a suicidal drunk, to a man proposing marriage to someone else while still married.
female_transformation: From a wife close to her brother-in-law to one pregnant, suspected and told by her husband's new attachment that he is cheating on her.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's summary breaks off with Deepa telling Sita that Ram is cheating on her.
relationship_analysis: One of the clearest cases in the filmography of the persona turned inside out: pair friction at eight against external opposition at six, with the Kapoor character as the sole author of the harm. Read beside Damini four years later, where he again plays a husband who fails his wife at the decisive moment, it marks the beginning of a recurring late-career role type.
critical_reading: The film is on Sita's side and never entertains the possibility that the suspicion is warranted, which is to its credit. Its resolution is another matter: the household is freed from the mother-in-law's cruelty by having the father-in-law beat her while the family applauds, so one domestic violence is cured by another and the film treats that as a happy turn.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the doctor who rescues him
how_they_meet: Ram gets drunk at a hotel and is rescued by Deepa, a doctor, who realises he is suicidal and decides to help him.
who_initiates: Ram, who begins to like her while she is treating him
courtship_pattern: Clinical before it is romantic: she withholds any rebuff deliberately until he is well enough to hear one, so the courtship is conducted inside a duty of care.
emotional_dynamic: Gratitude hardening into attachment on his side; professional judgement, then genuine sympathy, on hers.
pair_conflict: He is married, his wife is pregnant with his child, and he has told Deepa a version of events in which he is the injured party.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no quarrel between them; the corrosive element is the marriage he is concealing the truth about. Deepa's own decisions, delaying the rebuff and asking for time before answering the proposal, are careful rather than conflictual.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is Ram's marriage to Sita, and behind it Uma's insinuation, which is the reason he believes himself free to propose at all.
lover_boy_explanation: There is courtship here, and it is the one place in the film where Kapoor's character is warm, but it is a married man proposing on the strength of a suspicion he has not checked. The romantic register is real and its foundation is false.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The role gives Anita Raj the film's one genuinely deliberate character, a woman managing a patient's feelings rather than being swept into them, and the article's account gives her the decisive act.
actor_transformation: None; the proposal is the continuation of his error rather than a correction of it.
female_transformation: From the doctor who stopped him killing himself to the woman who goes to his wife and tells her the truth about him.
relationship_outcome: She asks for time to consider his proposal, then visits Sita and tells her that her husband is cheating on her.
relationship_analysis: The second relationship in one film and the one that begins to unwind the first: Deepa is the only character who acts on the information rather than hoarding it. Female agency at seven is unusually high for a second heroine of the period, and it is earned by her going to the wife rather than accepting the husband.
critical_reading: The film gives Deepa a profession, judgement and the moral courage to refuse a compromised proposal, which is more than the other-woman role usually receives. What it withholds is any reckoning for Ram: on the article's account he suffers nothing for proposing marriage while his wife is pregnant.

initial_relationship: Colleagues at a newspaper
how_they_meet: Radha is Vijay's co-worker at the newspaper he joins after his family is ruined; the article records that both fall in love.
courtship_pattern: Orthodox and approved, which is what makes its collapse remarkable: they seek and receive both families' blessings, and he then abandons it without explanation.
emotional_dynamic: Straightforward mutual love, destroyed from his side by a silence he never breaks.
pair_conflict: He severs all ties with her and marries another woman, letting her and everyone else conclude that he married for money.
pair_friction_explanation: The rupture is his act and it is total, but it is not a quarrel: he never tells her that the seven lakh he received was the exact sum his sister's dowry required. The friction is the unexplained abandonment, and it exists only because he chooses to bear the appearance of greed rather than shift the burden to her.
external_opposition_explanation: The framing of his father for diamond theft strips the family of its wealth and leaves his sister's marriage hanging on a seven lakh dowry no one can pay, and his father is paralysed by a stroke. The obstacle is not disapproval of Radha but a debt that can only be discharged by selling his own marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: The sacrifice is total and is made for love of his family rather than of Radha, which is the interesting complication: he gives up the woman he loves and accepts being thought mercenary to do it. Devotion, renunciation and silent suffering are all present; what is absent is any pursuit.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The relationship is written to be exemplary so that its abandonment lands, and the film keeps Radha off screen for much of the middle stretch, which limits what the pairing can build.
actor_transformation: From a young man in an approved love match to one who accepts the reputation of a fortune-hunter rather than explain himself.
female_transformation: Abandoned without a reason and left believing the man she loved married for money; restored to him only by his wife's dying request.
relationship_outcome: Reunited after Naina is killed and, before dying, asks Radha and Vijay to marry.
relationship_analysis: A structural inversion of the lover-boy pattern worth recording carefully: the hero performs the archetype's central act, sacrificing everything, but performs it against the romance rather than for it, and is punished by the audience's misreading as well as the characters'. Its resolution is also unusual in being granted by the other woman rather than won.
critical_reading: The film treats a dowry of seven lakh rupees as an unavoidable fact of life, and constructs its hero's nobility entirely inside that assumption; the practice itself is never questioned. Radha is given nothing to do but wait and be misinformed, and her reward is delivered by a dying woman's instruction rather than by any choice of her own.

initial_relationship: Employer's daughter; he works for her mother
how_they_meet: Naina is the only daughter of Shraddha, Vijay's boss at the newspaper; the marriage is transacted rather than courted.
who_initiates: Neither romantically; Vijay contracts the marriage for seven lakh rupees
courtship_pattern: None. The marriage is an exchange of money for a husband, and the article gives no courtship on either side.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented in the first instance; by the end she has enough regard for him to release him to the woman he loves.
pair_conflict: He married her for a sum of money he needed for his sister's dowry, and his heart is elsewhere throughout.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no recorded quarrel, but the marriage is founded on a transaction and on a concealed attachment to Radha. The friction is the falseness of the arrangement rather than hostility between them, and Naina's final act suggests she came to understand it.
external_opposition_explanation: The dowry demand that produced the marriage, and finally Dharamdas's goon, who kills her. Nothing opposes the marriage itself; the family circumstances are what created it.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor's character marries this woman for money while loving another, which is the negation of the archetype. There is no courtship and no devotion, and the only generosity in the relationship is hers at the end.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The part is largely functional until the death scene, which is where the article locates whatever weight Naina carries; Jaya Prada has the more interesting half of a thin role.
actor_transformation: None through this marriage; it is the price he pays rather than an experience that changes him.
female_transformation: From a boss's daughter bought a husband to a dying woman who hands him to the woman he actually loves.
relationship_outcome: Naina is killed by Dharamdas's goon, and asks Radha and Vijay to marry before she dies.
relationship_analysis: The second of two relationships in one film, and the mechanism by which the first is both destroyed and restored. Recording both separately shows the same character scoring eight on lover-boy in one relationship and two in the other within a single film, which is the clearest demonstration available that the score tracks the construction of a relationship rather than the actor's register.
critical_reading: Naina is purchased a husband by her mother, discovers she is a convenience, and is then killed so that the marriage she paid for can be dissolved without divorce. The film asks the audience to find her dying instruction touching, which requires overlooking that her entire function is to be an obstacle removed at the right moment.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the daughter of his family's servant
how_they_meet: Mala meets the head of the wealthy family her father Kishanlal serves, and he is so impressed by her that he asks for her hand for his fourth son Gopal; Kishanlal humbly accepts.
who_initiates: Neither; the patriarch arranges it on the strength of her character
courtship_pattern: None before the wedding. The relationship is built afterwards, and what builds it is that the two of them behave decently in a household where nobody else does.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and unforced from the start, and increasingly a pact against the rest of the family.
pair_conflict: None between them at any point.
pair_friction_explanation: The article records no conflict between Gopal and Mala. She is helpful and sweet-natured, he is the only brother who is decent, and they leave the house together; the marriage is the one stable thing in the film.
external_opposition_explanation: Three brothers and their abusive wives, who make the household intolerable, neglect their own mother, mortgage the family home and finally throw the old woman out before living off Gopal's earnings. Mala's origin as a servant's daughter in the same house is the standing class insult behind it.
lover_boy_explanation: Gopal is a devoted husband and the marriage is the centre of his life, but there is no courtship to perform and no opposition to the marriage itself to overcome. The devotion is domestic rather than romantic-heroic, which places it in the middle band.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Meenakshi Seshadri is top-billed and the film is named for her, so the pairing is written as a partnership of equals rather than a courtship; what it needs from the two of them is steadiness, which is what the article's account describes.
actor_transformation: From the youngest son deferring to his family to a man who leaves it and then confronts his brothers over their mother.
female_transformation: From a servant's daughter married into the house she might have worked in to a wife whose conduct is the film's standard for everyone else.
relationship_outcome: They move out together and build a life on his musical career; he discovers what his brothers did and confronts them.
relationship_analysis: One of the few marriages in the filmography that is simply good: friction at one, mutuality at eight, and a couple whose function is to be the moral baseline against which a family is measured. It also crosses the sharpest class line in the career, a servant's daughter married to the master's son inside the same house, and the film treats that as the marriage's strength rather than its problem.
critical_reading: The arrangement is still made entirely between men, a patriarch impressed by a girl and a father who humbly accepts, with Mala given no say in the marriage that defines her life. What the film does well is refuse the expected plot: her origins are never used against her by the man who married her, and the cruelty comes from the women who married in above her.

actress_character: Anita Kapoor, and the woman claiming to be her, Sujata Singh
actress_prominence: Female lead, credited in both identities
initial_relationship: Married, with a daughter
how_they_meet: They do not meet in the film. Ravi and Anita are on holiday in Kathmandu when the story opens, and she disappears from their hotel on the first night.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The film is not about a courtship but about a husband's certainty that the woman presented to him is not his wife.
emotional_dynamic: A marriage available to the audience only through his insistence on it, against a substitute who performs the role convincingly to everyone else.
pair_conflict: His wife is replaced by a stranger whom the whole world, including his own daughter, identifies as Anita.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no quarrel with Anita herself; the friction is the impossible position the substitution creates, in which maintaining the truth about his marriage makes him the prime suspect in his wife's disappearance. It is scored in the middle band because the relationship is under sustained attack from inside its own identity rather than from a rival.
external_opposition_explanation: An impostor is installed as his wife and corroborated by wedding photographs, the family doctor, a constable and finally his daughter, while Inspector Balveer Singh finds every piece of evidence pointing at Ravi. The conspiracy is total and is aimed precisely at the marriage's identity.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is a husband holding to a fact rather than a lover courting: there is no wooing, no rival for her affection and no romantic gesture. What the part requires is stubbornness under pressure, and the register is thriller rather than romance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The premise gives the couple almost no screen time together, since Anita vanishes in the first scene and Kimi Katkar spends the film playing the substitute; the marriage has to be taken on trust.
actor_transformation: From a husband reporting a disappearance to a man whose only remaining evidence is his own conviction, disbelieved by everyone including his child.
female_transformation: Not documented; Anita is absent for the film and the character on screen is the impostor.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's summary ends with Ravi still unable to prove the woman is not his wife.
relationship_analysis: A marriage used as the object of a gaslighting thriller rather than developed as a relationship, and the only pairing in the filmography in which the wife's identity, not her affection, is what is in dispute. One row records both credited identities because the plot treats them as a single contested position.
critical_reading: The film's interest is entirely in the husband's ordeal, and Anita exists as an absence to be argued over: she has no scenes, no agency and no account of her own disappearance within the article's summary. The most unsettling element, a daughter recruited to identify a stranger as her mother, is deployed as a plot escalation rather than examined.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he is her cousin's friend
how_they_meet: Chandni travels to Delhi with her parents for her cousin's wedding, where she meets Rohit, her cousin's friend; the article records that he falls in love with her instantly and begins courting her.
courtship_pattern: Relentless and extravagant on his side: continuous attempts until she accepts, an engagement, and finally a helicopter hired to shower her with rose petals, which is the gesture that destroys him.
emotional_dynamic: Exuberant and mutual, then severed by his shame, and finally rebuilt on her constancy rather than his.
pair_conflict: He releases her after his paralysis, judging himself unfit to be her husband, and she has to live with a decision she did not make.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple never quarrels, but the central rupture is Rohit's own act: he lets Chandni go. That is a decision taken inside the relationship rather than imposed on it, and it costs her years, which is why this scores above the near-zero readings of the 1970s romances.
external_opposition_explanation: The Guptas dislike Chandni on grounds of social status from the start, and after the crash they blame her for it and mistreat her, which is the injury she cites when refusing him later. The helicopter accident and his paralysis supply the rest, and Lalit's engagement to her becomes the final obstacle.
lover_boy_explanation: A full lover-boy construction for most of its length: instant love, persistent courtship, a grand romantic gesture, and then renunciation for her sake, which is the archetype's self-sacrificing form. It stops short of the top band because the decision that resolves the film is Lalit's rather than Rohit's, and because his renunciation is the thing Chandni most resents.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film is built to showcase Sridevi and Kapoor plays to that, with the courtship sequences carrying an unforced warmth that has to survive a long separation in the middle; the reunion scenes depend on the audience remembering the first half, which is the pairing's real test.
actor_transformation: From an exuberant suitor to a man who reads his own injury as disqualification and gives her away, and finally to one willing to ask a second time.
female_transformation: From a naive middle-class girl to a working woman in Mumbai who builds an independent life, accepts a second proposal on her own terms, and is honest about the grievance she holds against his family.
relationship_outcome: Chandni marries Rohit after Lalit sees her run to him and gives her up.
romantic_songs: 'Mere Haathon Mein Nau Nau Choodiyan', 'Lagi Aaj Sawan Ki', 'Tere Mere Hothon Pe', 'Main Sasural Nahi Jaoongi'
relationship_analysis: The last great romantic lead of Kapoor's career and the closing statement of the persona, thirty years after Bobby. The structure is the familiar one, a couple with little friction of their own against family and class opposition, but with an important variation: the wound is self-inflicted, and the years lost are lost because the hero decided for her. Chandni is also given far more independent life than the heroines of the 1970s films, working and choosing in the middle stretch rather than waiting.
critical_reading: The film's sympathy for Rohit's shame is genuine and its treatment of disability is of its time: paralysis is a disqualification from marriage that only recovery can lift, and the plot duly restores him before rewarding him. Against that, Chandni is allowed to say plainly what the Guptas did to her and to refuse on that basis, and her second engagement is not treated as a betrayal. Lalit's renunciation resolves the film, which means that once again the decisive act of love belongs to the man who loses.

initial_relationship: Married to each other in childhood, and strangers as adults
how_they_meet: They do not meet as adults until Deepak arrives at Kedarnath's house to claim Jyoti as the wife he was married to as a child, and moves in.
who_initiates: Deepak, by asserting the childhood marriage and installing himself in her family's home
courtship_pattern: None. The claim precedes any acquaintance and is enforced by residence rather than pursued by courtship.
emotional_dynamic: His assertion of a right against her open resentment; the article records the chagrin of Jyoti and her family at his arrival.
pair_conflict: She does not want the marriage, and he is living in her house on the strength of it.
pair_friction_explanation: The relationship is an unwanted claim pressed in person. Jyoti, her brother, her sister and her mother are all recorded as resenting his arrival, and there is no indication in the article that she is reconciled to it. The conflict is between the pair, not imposed on them.
external_opposition_explanation: Jyoti's wealthy family despises the poor Bhardwajs, and after Kedarnath's death her mother Sheela turns on both Deepak and the mistreated daughter-in-law Rani and orders them out of the house. The class gap is the reason the childhood marriage is an embarrassment to be repudiated.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no courtship, no devotion and no sacrifice; the character's romantic action is to arrive and claim a wife who does not want him. The role belongs to the same late-1980s group as Naseeb Apna Apna and Ek Chadar Maili Si, in which Kapoor plays men whose marriages are entitlements rather than attachments.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Third-billed in a crowded melodrama, Kapoor's thread is one of several and the article gives the relationship only its premise and the family's reaction to it.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the article's plot breaks off with him and Rani turned out of the house.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond her resentment at his arrival.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; after Kedarnath's death Sheela orders Deepak and Rani to leave.
relationship_analysis: A child marriage claimed in adulthood by the poorer party against a wealthy household's wishes, which makes the coercion and the class grievance point in opposite directions: he is both the wronged man and the one imposing himself. Recorded with low confidence because the article gives the premise and almost none of the development.
critical_reading: The film's sympathy appears to sit with Deepak as the poor relation despised by a rich family, which quietly requires the audience to set aside that the woman in question does not want the marriage. Her refusal is treated as snobbery rather than as a position with any merit of its own.

initial_relationship: Fellow students at law college
how_they_meet: They are classmates at law college, where the article records Bharati as already in love with her fellow collegian Vijay when the film opens.
who_initiates: Mutual; the attachment predates the plot
courtship_pattern: Barely a courtship at all. The relationship is established at the outset and immediately converts into a partnership against her father, so what the film shows is collaboration rather than wooing.
emotional_dynamic: Steady and practical: he is the person she takes to Goa to verify what she has been told about her father, and the person who fights her case at the end.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Vijay and Bharati is recorded at any point. Every pressure on the relationship comes from her family and the conspiracy around it, and the two act in concert throughout.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father Ashok made his fortune smuggling and selling children and young women, and holds documents that would deliver the country to a foreign power. The couple's attempt to stop him leads to Vijay's reported death, the deaths of both her parents, a murder charge against her, and a conspiracy involving her uncle and a minister to have her declared insane.
lover_boy_explanation: The devotion is real and materially expressed, going with her to Goa, recovering the documents, saving her and finally arguing her case in court, but the register is that of an ally rather than a suitor. There is no courtship, no rivalry and no sacrifice specifically for love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The article's plot is garbled and gives the couple little direct interaction, but the structure it describes is unusually balanced, with Bharati driving the investigation and Vijay supporting it.
actor_transformation: From a law student in love to a lawyer conducting her defence against a minister.
female_transformation: From a wealthy student who believes her father to a woman who kills him, flees with the evidence, survives an attempt to certify her mad, and prosecutes the minister behind it.
relationship_outcome: They fight the case against the minister together; the article's account has Vijay saving her and killing the minister during the attack outside the court.
relationship_analysis: One of the most equal partnerships in the filmography, with mutuality and female agency both at eight: Bharati does the discovering, the killing and the testifying, and Vijay assists. It is also the clearest case of a Kapoor romance in which the opposition is political rather than domestic, since what stands between them is a trafficking network with a minister behind it.
critical_reading: The film gives Rekha's character an extraordinary amount to do by the standards of a 1990 masala thriller, including the moral centre and the decisive violence, and treats her sanity as the thing the villains most need to destroy. The article's own account is internally contradictory about whether Vijay dies, which makes it impossible to say how much of the resolution the film actually grants him.

initial_relationship: Strangers of very unequal standing
how_they_meet: Not documented in detail; after the serpents install Bhola in a mansion and train him into courage, he falls in love with Kamini, the daughter of the wealthy Seth Lalchand.
courtship_pattern: Enabled entirely by supernatural patronage: Bhola can court her at all only because Bhanu has given him wealth and Pritam has trained him out of timidity.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual attachment, presented as the reward for his transformation rather than as a relationship examined in its own right.
pair_conflict: None between them; her father has promised her elsewhere.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Bhola and Kamini is recorded. The obstruction is her father's plan to marry her to his business partner Vikram, and the wizard he sets on Bhola.
external_opposition_explanation: Seth Lalchand, an animal trafficker and the wizard Aghori's disciple, intends Kamini for his business partner Vikram and asks Aghori to destroy Bhola, who is poisoned by a bite and survives only because Bhanu draws the venom out. The wedding to Vikram is in progress when Bhola breaks in.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is the goal of Bhola's whole transformation and he crashes the wedding to claim her, which is the archetype's classic move. It scores in the middle band because he achieves none of it under his own power: the wealth, the courage and the survival are all supplied by the serpent deities.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film's energy is in the serpent-and-wizard plot rather than in the romance, and the article treats Kamini largely as the prize the transformation is for.
actor_transformation: From a bullied, suicidal villager into a man of means and courage, though the change is done to him rather than achieved by him.
female_transformation: Not documented; she is promised to one man and claimed by another.
relationship_outcome: Bhola breaks into the wedding with Pritam; the film ends happily with the serpents ascending.
relationship_analysis: A conventional forbidden-love romance grafted onto a mythological fantasy, notable mainly for how completely the hero's romantic capacity is outsourced: everything that makes him eligible is a gift from the supernatural couple whose lives he once saved. Rekha is billed high but plays his sister, so the female billing is a poor guide to the romance here.
critical_reading: Kamini has no recorded preference of her own until the hero arrives to take her from the wedding her father arranged, and the film's interest in her is exhausted by her availability. The more interesting relationship in the film is between the two serpents, who have a marriage, a debt and a choice.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she finds him washed ashore with no memory
how_they_meet: Henna comes across an unconscious man on the bank of the Jhelum in Pakistani Kashmir. She, her father Khan Baba and the village doctor Gul Bibi nurse him back to health and find he has lost his memory, and they call him Chand after the name he cries out in his sleep.
courtship_pattern: Domestic and gradual: he recovers in her household, works with the village doctor making clay pots, and the attachment grows inside a family that has taken him in as a stranger with no past.
emotional_dynamic: Tender and uncomplicated on both sides, and built entirely on a man who does not know who he is.
pair_conflict: None between them. The catastrophe is that his identity returns.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no conflict between Henna and Chand at any point. The film's entire pressure is external, and the relationship is destroyed by a fact rather than by a disagreement: on the morning of the wedding he remembers that he is an Indian Hindu with a fiancée.
external_opposition_source: Religion; Community; War or politics; Fate
external_opposition_explanation: A militarised border, two religions and two nationalities; the suspicion of the Pakistani police that he is an Indian spy; Daroga Shahbaaz Khan, who has already married twice and may marry twice more under Shariat law and who wants Henna; one of her own brothers colluding with him to foil the first escape. The opposition kills her.
lover_boy_explanation: The devotion is genuine but the role is unusually passive for the archetype: with no memory, Chand cannot pursue, choose or rebel, and once his memory returns his obligation runs the other way. The romantic heroism in the second half is Henna's, not his; she dies getting him home.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film was conceived by Raj Kapoor and completed by Randhir Kapoor after his death, and the casting of the Pakistani actress Zeba Bakhtiar opposite Kapoor is the point of it; the relationship has to carry the film's argument about the border, and the gentleness of the playing is what makes the ending land.
actor_transformation: From a man with no name, happy in a borrowed life, to one whose recovered identity destroys the household that saved him.
female_transformation: From a woman who takes in a stranger to one who defies a predatory official and her own brother to get him across the border, and dies doing it.
relationship_outcome: The second attempt to return him to India succeeds, and Henna loses her life in the chaos; the article records the film ending with Chandar asking why there must be war.
romantic_songs: 'Der Na Ho Jaye', 'Main Hoon Khush Rang Henna', 'Chitthiye Dard Firaq Waaliye'
relationship_analysis: The last great tragic romance of the career and the one that puts the pattern to political use: friction at one, opposition at ten, with the obstacle a national border rather than a father. Read against Laila Majnu fifteen years earlier, the structure is identical and the meaning is transposed from legend to geopolitics, which is the clearest measure of how the persona aged.
critical_reading: The film's plea against the border is made through a Muslim Pakistani woman who saves an Indian Hindu man and dies for it, and the asymmetry is worth naming: she gives up her life and he returns to his fiancée. Henna is nonetheless the most active of the three heroines in Kapoor's late romances, driving the rescue against both a coercive official and her own family, and the film gives her the title and the moral weight.

initial_relationship: Engaged, and about to be married
how_they_meet: Not documented; the engagement is established when the film opens and he calls her 'Chand'.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The relationship exists as the settled life the accident interrupts, and the article gives it no development.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented in detail; her hold on him is strong enough that her name is what he cries in his sleep with no memory.
pair_conflict: He disappears on the day of their engagement and spends the film in another country, about to marry someone else.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is recorded. The separation is an accident and his near-marriage to Henna happens while he has no knowledge of Chandni's existence, so nothing in the rupture is chosen.
external_opposition_explanation: A car accident carries him across the line of control into Pakistan, and amnesia removes her from his mind entirely. The border and the suspicion of espionage keep him there.
lover_boy_explanation: The devotion is involuntary and touching, since her name survives in him when nothing else does, but he takes no action for this relationship at any point: he cannot, because he does not know it exists. The score records a real attachment with no agency attached to it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Ashwini Bhave has very little screen time against the title role, and the relationship works as a premise rather than a performance; its one powerful moment is offstage, in the name he calls out while unconscious.
actor_transformation: None in relation to Chandni; he loses her from his memory entirely and recovers her as a fact rather than through any change in himself.
female_transformation: Not documented; she waits.
relationship_outcome: He returns to India at the cost of Henna's life; the article does not record the state of this engagement at the close.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the engagement is the film's premise and the name 'Chand' is the thread that runs through the whole plot, but it is the thinner of the film's two relationships by a wide margin. Its function is to make the Henna romance impossible, which it does simply by existing.
