critical_reading: Chandni is an obligation rather than a character: she is engaged, abandoned by accident, and waiting at the end, with no recorded action of her own. The film spends its sympathy on the woman who dies and leaves the woman who waited entirely unexamined.

initial_relationship: Strangers drawn to each other without explanation
how_they_meet: The Banjara tribe camps on land owned by Kumar Singh's father, and the two feel what the article calls an unknown attraction towards each other; Reshma's recurring nightmare of being hunted to death stops from the moment he arrives.
who_initiates: Neither; the attraction is presented as the pull of a previous life
courtship_pattern: Compressed and fugitive: an immediate mutual recognition, both families' armed objection, and an elopement to an abandoned haveli within the film's first movement.
emotional_dynamic: Absolute and unexplained to the participants, who do not know they are completing something interrupted decades earlier.
pair_conflict: None between them at any point.
pair_friction_explanation: Kumar and Reshma are never divided. The film's premise is that their union is the resolution of an old wrong, so the couple functions as a single unit against everything ranged outside it.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father, the tribe's leader, is angry because she is already engaged to Shakti Singh; his father, the Rana, objects to his only son pursuing a nomad girl; both arrive at the haveli with armed men. Behind that sits the first life, in which the caretaker himself killed the lower-class Suraj and his daughter Devi took her own life.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is built on romantic devotion against class prohibition and armed fathers, and he elopes with her rather than yield. It stops short of the top band because the resolution is delivered by Thakur Baba's revelation rather than won by the lovers, who are rescued by an old man's confession.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The third Kapoor and Sridevi pairing, after Nagina (1986) and Chandni (1989), and the premise requires the attraction to read as involuntary and pre-existing rather than as courtship, which suits a register both had already established together.
actor_transformation: From a landowner's son to a man who leaves his father's house for a nomad girl and is told he has done it once before.
female_transformation: From a woman haunted nightly by her own murder to one who learns the dream was a memory and outlives it.
relationship_outcome: The feud ends when Thakur Baba pleads for them with the account of their previous lives, and the two are allowed to live together.
relationship_analysis: Mutuality at nine is among the highest in the filmography, because the premise makes the attachment symmetrical by construction: both partners are reincarnations of the same interrupted couple. It is also Kapoor's second reincarnation romance after Karz, with the significant difference that here the previous life belongs to both of them rather than to him alone.
critical_reading: The film resolves a caste-and-class prohibition not by arguing against it but by producing a supernatural exemption, which lets both fathers relent without conceding anything about the principle. The most striking figure is Thakur Baba, who murdered the lower-class boy in the first life and pleads for him in the second; the film grants him the resolution and never asks him to answer for the killing.

initial_relationship: Strangers introduced as an arranged match
how_they_meet: Divya's father tells her to come home early from college to meet Vijay, the prospective groom. She deliberately arrives late hoping he will have gone, and finds him still patiently waiting.
who_initiates: Vijay, by declining to be driven off
courtship_pattern: Entirely after the wedding, and conducted as forbearance rather than pursuit: he does not touch her, listens to the whole history of the man she loved, and then puts the choice in her hands.
emotional_dynamic: Her open unwillingness against his refusal to take offence at it; he is the only person in the film who does not pressure her.
pair_conflict: She does not want him, is still in love with a man shot dead in front of her, and asks for a divorce as her wedding gift.
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is substantial and located wholly inside the couple: a wife who tries to make her husband dislike her, refuses the marriage, will not consummate it and asks for a divorce. It is not hostility, and none of it is his doing, but it is interpersonal rather than external, and it is what the film is about.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father's heart attack and her mother's plea are what force the marriage, and the law then refuses the divorce for a year because they are newly married. In the flashback, the police shooting of Suraj on their wedding day is the wound everything else follows from. Nobody opposes Vijay and Divya as a couple.
lover_boy_explanation: The devotion is real, patient and unusually decent: he waits, absorbs the rudeness, hears her out, and offers the divorce rather than extract a consent. But he neither courts nor pursues, and the archetype's ardour is entirely absent; what the role supplies instead is restraint.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Neelam is top-billed and the film is hers; Kapoor's part requires him to hold the screen doing almost nothing, which is a different demand from any of his 1970s romances and the reason this is among the more interesting late leading roles.
actor_transformation: From a suitor who will not be insulted away to a husband who offers his wife the divorce she asked for rather than hold her to a consent she never gave.
female_transformation: From a woman who lost her life's love in front of her and married under duress to one given a genuine choice and a year in which to make it.
relationship_outcome: Divya chooses the divorce papers over the anklets, and the law compels the couple to live together for a year before it can be filed.
relationship_analysis: The most striking score inversion in the filmography: pair friction at seven against external opposition at four, in a career whose signature is the reverse. It is also the clearest instance of Kapoor playing consent rather than conquest, and female agency at eight is earned by the film actually letting Divya choose divorce rather than overruling her.
critical_reading: A remake of Mouna Ragam, and it keeps the original's real subject: a woman compelled into a marriage and a husband who declines to treat the compulsion as a licence. The film's ethics are notably better than the period's norm, since it treats the unconsummated marriage as correct rather than as a humiliation to be remedied. What it cannot escape is the structure that traps her anyway, with the law rather than a family enforcing a year of cohabitation she did not choose.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is a stage dancer and he a pickpocket
how_they_meet: Not documented in detail; the article records that Vijay falls for Seema, a stage dancer.
courtship_pattern: Expressed through theft: he gives her a necklace stolen from a house that turns out to be his own brother's, and the gift is what sets the film's injustice in motion.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented beyond the courtship gesture and its consequences.
pair_conflict: His gift is stolen property, and its discovery on stage exposes them both.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is recorded. The difficulty is that his courtship is conducted with stolen goods, which lands an innocent woman in prison and forces his public confession.
external_opposition_explanation: The theft, the wrongful imprisonment of his brother's wife Sharda, and Kalicharan's conspiracy around the amnesiac Rajesh, which culminates in the abduction of most of the family.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is the occasion for the plot rather than its subject, and Vijay's defining acts are fraternal: confessing to spare Sharda, taking the pregnant and disowned woman back to their village, and recognising his brother from a portrait. Romance is a strand the film sets aside.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The first of eleven films with Juhi Chawla across thirty years, and the article's compressed prose gives the relationship its premise and its consequence but nothing of its texture.
actor_transformation: From a thief courting a dancer with stolen goods to the man who confesses publicly and then reassembles his family.
female_transformation: Not documented; she is caught on stage wearing the stolen necklace and the article does not follow her further.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot resolves the family reunion without stating the outcome of the romance.
relationship_analysis: A minor romance whose importance is mechanical: the stolen necklace given as a courtship gift is what imprisons an innocent woman and forces the confession that begins the family's reassembly. It is recorded for that reason rather than for any development of the relationship.
critical_reading: Seema is the recipient of a gift and then the occasion of an exposure, with no recorded position of her own on either. The article's account is compressed to the point of obscurity in places, and the film's attention is plainly on the brothers.

initial_relationship: Strangers who marry early in the film
how_they_meet: Not documented in detail; the article records that Kajal falls in love with Ravi, a rich and handsome man, and that they marry happily with his mother Lakshmi Devi's blessing.
courtship_pattern: Brief and approved, and over within the first movement: the film spends its length not on the courtship but on what happens to the marriage after he is presumed dead.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and sanctioned, then reduced to her widowhood and finally to the impossible position of his being alive.
pair_conflict: None between them. He is thrown off a cliff by relatives who stand to inherit, and returns to find her remarried.
pair_friction_explanation: Ravi and Kajal are never in conflict. Every obstruction is external: an attempted murder, a presumed death, and a second marriage contracted in good faith while he was gone.
external_opposition_explanation: His uncle Dhirendra and cousin Narendra are next in line for the family fortune and hire men to kill him, which puts him over a cliff and makes her a widow. Raja's father then objects to his son marrying a widow, and by the time Ravi resurfaces the second marriage is a fact. Dhirendra finally kidnaps Kajal and Raja to extort the property.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi is a romantic lead in the first movement and is written sympathetically thereafter, but the film hands the lover-boy function to Shah Rukh Khan's Raja, who does the pursuing, the persisting and the defying of a father. Kapoor's part becomes the obstacle rather than the suitor, which is a notable transfer given his own screen history.
chemistry_explanation: The article cites Rachit Gupta of Filmfare, writing in 2014, that Divya Bharti seemed at ease sharing screen space with Kapoor, and records a reviewer praising the performances of both. This is one of very few pairings in the filmography with any located critical comment on the playing rather than an interpretive reading, and what it describes is ease rather than charge.
actor_transformation: From an untroubled bridegroom to a man whose survival is an inconvenience to the woman he loves and a friend he made without knowing who he was.
female_transformation: From a bride to a widow to a woman persuaded into a second marriage by her mother-in-law, and then confronted with a first husband who is not dead.
relationship_outcome: Kajal stays with Raja after learning Ravi survived; the article's plot then has Dhirendra kidnap her and Raja to extort Ravi's property, and breaks off there.
romantic_songs: 'Teri Ummeed Tera Intezar', 'Aisi Deewangi', 'Payaliya'
relationship_analysis: A structurally significant pairing: Kapoor plays the first husband whose return threatens a remarriage, and the romantic-hero function passes visibly to Shah Rukh Khan in his debut. The film also revisits widow remarriage ten years after Prem Rog, with Kapoor now on the opposite side of the arrangement, which makes the two films a useful pair for tracking how his position in a romance changed.
critical_reading: Lakshmi Devi's argument for the second marriage is unusually practical for the period, that Kajal is young, childless and will be alone, and the film treats the remarriage as right rather than as a lapse. Kajal's decision to stay with Raja once Ravi resurfaces is also allowed to stand, which is more agency than the situation usually grants a heroine. What the article's account leaves unresolved is what the film finally does with the first husband.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he comes to her village on business
how_they_meet: Kishan travels to a village to look into business prospects and meets Radha, a village belle; alongside his work he begins teaching English to her and others, and the two slowly fall in love.
who_initiates: Mutual, growing out of the lessons
courtship_pattern: Conducted through teaching, which gives the courtship a pretext and a rhythm; he leaves with a promise to return, and everything afterwards is about that promise being impersonated.
emotional_dynamic: Unhurried and mutual, then tested by her believing he has forgotten her while an impostor wears his face.
pair_conflict: She sees a man she takes to be Kishan partying with other women and concludes he has abandoned her.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no real conflict between Kishan and Radha; the apparent betrayal she witnesses is Tony Montana, not him. The friction is entirely a product of the substitution, and it is dispelled as soon as the real Kishan can reach her and explain.
external_opposition_explanation: An exact double takes Kishan's identity, his house and his business, backed by the cousin he had banished for fraud; the impostor knows about Radha, his own dog goes to the double, he is thrown out of his home and arrested at his own office, and his mother has been killed in what he comes to suspect was no accident.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is charming and central to the first half, and the romance is one of the two things he is fighting to recover, alongside his name. It sits in the middle band because the second half is a thriller about identity in which Radha becomes an ally rather than an object of pursuit.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The second of eleven Kapoor and Juhi Chawla films, and the double-role premise asks him to be both the man she loves and the man she thinks has betrayed her, with her recognition of the difference as the hinge.
actor_transformation: From an industrialist secure in his name to a man with no proof he is himself, whose only remaining credential is that Radha believes him.
female_transformation: From a village girl learning English to a woman who travels to the city, is deceived by a double, and then joins the plan to expose him.
relationship_outcome: He stops her leaving, explains the substitution, and the two of them with the escaped convict Goonga go to Goa to expose Tony Montana.
romantic_songs: 'Tu Tu Tu Tu Tara', 'Bol Radha Bol'
relationship_analysis: A courtship built on teaching and then attacked by impersonation, so the romance becomes the film's test of identity: the dog is fooled, the household is fooled, and Radha is the one who can be brought to see the difference. Recording it as manipulated by outsiders rather than as deception is deliberate, since the lie is told about him rather than by him.
critical_reading: The film gives Radha an active part in the recovery rather than leaving her to be won back, and her initial conclusion that he has forgotten her is treated as reasonable rather than as faithlessness. The class and city-village gap between them is used for comedy and never becomes an obstacle, which is unusual for the pattern.

initial_relationship: Strangers who meet on holiday
how_they_meet: Dushyant travels to a hill station on holiday and runs into Shakuntala, who falls in love with him.
who_initiates: Shakuntala, entirely and against his resistance
courtship_pattern: Reversed: she pursues a man sworn to bachelorhood, he rebuffs her, she persists, and he reciprocates only after her persistence has worn the vow down.
emotional_dynamic: Her open determination against his evasion, and once he yields, a shared problem in the form of his uncle.
pair_conflict: He has promised his uncle he will never marry and rebuffs her on the strength of it.
pair_friction_explanation: The rebuffs are real and repeated, and they come from him. It is not hostility but a standing refusal she has to overcome, which is friction located inside the pair rather than imposed on it.
external_opposition_explanation: Professor Vishwamitra, who runs an association of confirmed single men, extracted the vow and is upset when it is broken; he then falls in love with Shakuntala himself, which turns the guardian into the rival. His parents, unusually, are on the side of the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor spends the first half of the film refusing romance rather than pursuing it, which is the archetype's opposite, and the courtship energy belongs to Urmila Matondkar. He scores in the middle band because once he yields he commits against his uncle, but nothing in the role is organised around wooing.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The comedy depends on her being more forceful than he is, and the article's account gives her every initiative in the relationship.
actor_transformation: From a man defined by a promise never to marry to one who breaks it against the person he made it to.
female_transformation: Not documented; her persistence is constant from her first appearance.
relationship_outcome: The article records that Dushyant and Shakuntala end up together.
relationship_analysis: One of very few films in the filmography in which the woman is the pursuer throughout and the Kapoor character the reluctant party. Female agency at eight is earned by the structure rather than by anything the film says about her: she does all the courting, and his arc is simply to stop refusing.
critical_reading: The premise, an association of men vowed against marriage, is played as farce and the film's sympathies are with the woman battering it down. The uncle's late infatuation with the same woman is the one element that turns uncomfortable, since it makes her the object of a contest between nephew and guardian rather than a party to her own courtship.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he sees her perform
how_they_meet: Shekhar falls in love at first sight after watching Damini's dance performance at a charity event.
courtship_pattern: Brief and untroubled, and over within the film's opening movement: he marries her across a sharp class divide and she moves into the Gupta bungalow. Everything that matters happens afterwards.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine affection on both sides, progressively unable to survive what his family requires of her.
pair_conflict: She witnesses his brother and his friends gang-raping the family's maid and resolves to testify; he asks her not to speak to the police, and then cannot protect her from his family's lawyer.
pair_friction_explanation: The rupture is squarely between them: Shekhar tries to talk his wife out of going to the police, which puts him on his family's side at the decisive moment. He objects to what they do to her afterwards and never acts against them, and she is committed to a mental institution on his family's motion while he is still objecting. That is conflict inside the marriage, not opposition from outside it.
external_opposition_explanation: The Gupta family conspires to bury the rape; Tolu Bajaj bribes the police to escalate it in order to damage them; the barrister Chaddha portrays Damini in court as mentally unstable and has her confined by judicial order for two weeks; and inside the institution Rakesh asks a doctor to make her genuinely ill or kill her and pass it off as suicide.
lover_boy_explanation: The film opens with a full romantic gesture, love at first sight and a marriage across class, and then systematically dismantles it. Shekhar's defining acts are failures of nerve rather than devotion, and the man who actually fights for Damini is a stranger, the alcoholic advocate Govind. The score records real initial ardour against a role whose function is insufficiency.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The part requires Kapoor to be sympathetic and inadequate at once, a husband the audience believes loves his wife and still watches him fail her, and the early courtship has to be warm enough to make the later collapse land.
actor_transformation: From an ardent husband to a man whose decency is exhausted by objecting to his family while his wife is institutionalised.
female_transformation: From a woman who raises her voice against injustice to one who acts on it at the cost of her home, her liberty and nearly her life, and who escapes the institution alone.
relationship_outcome: Not documented in full; the article records Shekhar becoming upset with his family while the Guptas and Bajaj reconcile, and Damini escaping and finding Govind.
relationship_analysis: Female agency at nine is the highest reading in the filmography, and it is earned against her husband rather than with him: Damini's every consequential act is taken in opposition to the family Shekhar will not break with. The pairing is the fullest statement of the role type Kapoor occupied through the 1990s, the decent husband who is not equal to the moment, which runs from Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani through Saajan Ka Ghar to this.
critical_reading: The film is unambiguous that the cover-up is monstrous and that the courts and psychiatry are available as instruments of it, which is why it endured. Its treatment of Shekhar is its most interesting choice: he is not a villain and is never redeemed either, and the film declines to let marital affection count as a defence. The rape of the maid Urmi remains a device, and she is given far less interiority than the wife who witnesses it.

initial_relationship: Not documented
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records only that Krishna loves Pinky and marries her.
courtship_pattern: Not documented. The marriage is stated in a single clause and the film's attention is on the two brothers and the returning father.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Krishna and Pinky is recorded. Scored low and provisionally: the article gives the marriage a clause and no development.
external_opposition_explanation: Krishna's biological father Veerendra returns from prison and schemes to split the two brothers over their inheritance, which threatens the household the marriage sits inside. Nothing is aimed at the marriage itself.
lover_boy_explanation: The marriage is settled before the plot engages and produces no courtship, devotion or sacrifice. Kapoor's role is organised around the adoptive brotherhood and the returning father.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, and the article documents almost nothing of it. There is not enough recorded interaction to judge.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's resolution concerns the brothers and Jyoti rather than this marriage.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the article states the marriage directly, but scored thinly throughout. Its only structural interest is the contrast with the film's other couple, Sunny Deol's Jeet and Juhi Chawla's Jyoti, who carry the romance the film is actually interested in.
critical_reading: Too little survives to read the film's framing. Pinky is identified in the cast list by her relationships to two men, her husband and her maternal uncle, and the article adds nothing to that.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is abducted by his companion
how_they_meet: Deeka kidnaps Meena, the daughter of DCP Ujwal Raja Bully, as leverage while trying to force Eena to confess and clear his name; Eena and Meena fall in love afterwards.
who_initiates: Not documented; the attachment forms during her captivity
courtship_pattern: Begins with her abduction and proceeds in flight, so the courtship is conducted between a hostage and one of the two men holding her.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented beyond the fact of the attachment and its improbable origin.
pair_conflict: She is a captive and he is a bank robber unwilling to confess to the crime that put them all in flight.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is recorded, and the film treats the situation comically. The friction is the circumstance rather than anything between the two, which is why it is scored low despite the abduction.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father is a Deputy Commissioner of Police pursuing them; Bhujang, who kidnapped Deeka as a child, wants his own son Sunny to marry Meena; and a police manhunt runs under the whole romance.
lover_boy_explanation: Eena's governing motive is money for his mother's treatment and then avoiding the confession that would clear Deeka. The romance arrives late and is resolved by the plot's general amnesty rather than by anything he does for it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The fourth of eleven Kapoor and Juhi Chawla films, three of them released in 1994 alone, and the David Dhawan register asks for broad comic playing rather than romantic charge.
actor_transformation: From a selfish incompetent who will not own his crime to a man restored to a brother and married.
female_transformation: Not documented; she moves from hostage to bride without a recorded change.
relationship_outcome: Eena and Meena marry once Bhujang and his sons are arrested and Deeka is reunited with the family.
relationship_analysis: A comedy romance whose origin is an abduction, recorded because the article states both the kidnapping and the subsequent love plainly. It belongs with Barood (1976) among the small group of films in which a Kapoor character's romance begins in the instrumental use of a woman, though here the instrument is his brother's rather than his own.
critical_reading: The film treats the kidnapping of a police officer's daughter as a comic premise and her falling in love with one of her captors as an unremarkable development, which is the period's convention and reads poorly now. Meena is given no recorded response to her own abduction.

initial_relationship: Strangers married by her father and stepmother
how_they_meet: They do not meet before the wedding. Laxmi's father Dhanraj and her stepmother, who have mistreated her since her birth, arrange her marriage to Amar, an army officer.
who_initiates: Neither; the marriage is arranged by the family that wanted rid of her
courtship_pattern: None. The film begins the relationship at the wedding and is concerned with a medical secret and its consequences rather than with courtship.
emotional_dynamic: Affection constrained by a fact he will not tell her, and then by his flight from what the concealment produced.
pair_conflict: After her miscarriage he is told she will die if she carries another pregnancy to term, and decides to tell nobody, including her; she overhears, resolves to have a child anyway, and provokes him into the night that will kill her.
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is entirely internal and largely his: a concealment that deprives her of the one fact she most needed, followed by a night he was provoked into and was horrified by, followed by his departure for duty instead of consulting a doctor or discussing an abortion. His mother's murder plot is external, but the marriage's wound is his own.
external_opposition_explanation: Her own father and stepmother abused her from birth and blamed her for her brother's amputation; Amar's mother plots her murder when she does not conceive, and later slaps her and throws her out of the house, after which she works in the village and sleeps in a barn. The medical condition itself is the other implacable fact.
lover_boy_explanation: Amar's intention towards his wife is protective and the concealment is meant kindly, but nothing in the role is courtship, devotion or sacrifice, and his decisive act is to leave. The register is a husband failing rather than a lover.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Juhi Chawla is first-billed and the film is Laxmi's ordeal; Kapoor's part is to be well-meaning and absent, which gives the pairing little to build on by design.
actor_transformation: From a husband protecting his wife by silence to one whose silence produced the pregnancy that will kill her, and who goes off to duty rather than face it.
female_transformation: From a woman mistreated by her own family into a marriage to one who chooses a fatal pregnancy as the only decision available to her, and is then thrown out to sleep in a barn.
relationship_outcome: Not documented in full; he departs for duty and the article follows Laxmi, evicted by his mother and giving birth alone.
relationship_analysis: The most severe of the 1990s failing-husband roles: pair friction at seven with external opposition at eight, and a wife worse off at every stage of the marriage. What distinguishes it from Damini is that here the husband's failure is an act of intended kindness, which the film shows producing a worse outcome than candour would have.
critical_reading: The article's own account is damning without editorialising: rather than consult a doctor or discuss a termination, Amar leaves for duty. The film's melodramatic machinery treats Laxmi's decision to risk death for a child as noble womanhood, which is the framing to resist; read now, it is a woman with no other means of asserting anything, handed a fatal choice because her husband would not give her a fact.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she arrives as an unwanted encumbrance
how_they_meet: Sapna runs away from her aristocratic home, fed up with the hatred and family politics in it, and meets Raj, to whom she is attracted.
who_initiates: Sapna, by attaching herself to him; his first instinct is to get rid of her
courtship_pattern: The reluctant-host pattern of Roman Holiday: he wants her off his hands, keeps her anyway, and falls in love in the course of trying to be rid of her, after which the courtship becomes a flight.
emotional_dynamic: Her interest against his irritation, resolving into a shared predicament once her family starts hunting her.
pair_conflict: He does not want her there and spends the first stretch trying to hand her back.
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is his resistance to her presence, which is real and sustained before it converts. It is comic rather than hostile, and it sits inside the pair rather than being imposed on it.
external_opposition_explanation: The aristocratic household she fled puts up a reward for information on her whereabouts, which turns the relationship into a pursuit and forces the pair onto the run; Amrish Puri and Gulshan Grover play the family's enforcers.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor begins the film trying to get rid of the heroine, which is the archetype's opposite, and ends it in flight with her against her family, which is the archetype's classic position. The score sits in the middle to record both halves.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The structure requires a comic antagonism to carry the first half and warmth to carry the second, and the article's account describes exactly that progression without commenting on the playing.
actor_transformation: From a man trying to return a runaway to the family she escaped to one running from that family beside her.
female_transformation: From a woman fleeing a household of hatred and politics to one with somewhere and someone to flee towards.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's summary ends with the two of them on the run from her family.
relationship_analysis: Recovered late in this research, because the article keeps its plot under a Summary heading the extraction script does not read; without it the film would have been recorded as undocumented. The pairing is one of the few in the filmography where the heroine's flight, not the hero's pursuit, sets the romance going, and where he has to be talked round rather than she.
critical_reading: Sapna is given the film's only decisive act before the romance starts, leaving a family she found intolerable, and the plot then makes her a fugitive with a price on her location. The Roman Holiday borrowing is inverted in one important respect: there the runaway returns to her duty, while here the aristocratic family is simply the antagonist.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he is a waiter and she a performer
how_they_meet: Raju, having run away from his father's palace to Bombay and taken work as a waiter, meets Anita, a dancer and singer and the daughter of a wealthy man, and falls in love with her.
courtship_pattern: Conducted entirely under a suppressed identity: she believes she is being courted by a waiter, and the concealment of his rank is what eventually ruptures it.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and unforced until the disclosure, after which her anger is at having been kept in the dark rather than at what he turned out to be.
pair_conflict: He never tells her he is the heir to Ramgarh, and she learns it from a rival.
pair_friction_explanation: The rupture is a concealment of his own choosing, revealed by Jimmy Narang at the worst moment, and her anger is directed at Raju for suppressing it. That is friction between the partners, distinct from the fathers' opposition operating around them.
external_opposition_explanation: His father has already arranged his marriage to a woman of noble parentage and sets off with an army to fetch him back for it; her father intends her for Jimmy Narang, son of the wealthy Mr. Narang, and Narang is the one who informs the Maharaj where Raju is.
lover_boy_explanation: Raju leaves a palace, takes work as a waiter and refuses an arranged royal marriage for a singer he met in Bombay, which is the archetype's substance. It falls short of the top band because the deception is his and because the article leaves him choosing between capture and further flight rather than acting.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film is a transposition of Coming to America and the romance carries its comic premise, a man of rank passing as a servant, rather than a distinctive charge of its own.
actor_transformation: From a prince kept in seclusion by a prophecy to a waiter who would rather keep running than accept the marriage arranged for him.
female_transformation: From a performer courted by a waiter to a woman who discovers she was never told who she was being courted by.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with Raju facing the choice between capture by his father's men and flight.
relationship_analysis: A late variation on the false-identity courtships that run through the 1970s work, from Rafoo Chakkar to Jhoota Kahin Ka, with the significant difference that here the concealment is of rank rather than of poverty or criminality, and the woman's grievance is treated as legitimate. Shammi Kapoor plays the opposing father, one of several films pairing the two as father and son.
critical_reading: The film gives Anita a real objection, that she was courted by a man who withheld who he was, and lets her be angry about it rather than flattered. Against that, both fathers are transacting her future between them and the resolution the article reaches is about what Raju will do, not what she will.

initial_relationship: Members of the same joint household; she is his sister-in-law's younger sister and a child widow
how_they_meet: They are already living in the same joint family when the film opens, Geeta having come to the house as the younger sister of Seeta, the eldest brother's wife.
who_initiates: Mutual; the article records that they always dispute and are in love
courtship_pattern: Conducted as bickering inside a shared household, and interrupted when the family's new wives use her widowhood to have her expelled.
emotional_dynamic: Quarrelsome affection, and then a separation neither of them chooses.
pair_conflict: None of substance; the disputes are the form the attachment takes.
pair_friction_explanation: The article describes constant dispute alongside constant love, which places this in the playful register rather than the damaging one. Nothing divides them by their own choice.
external_opposition_explanation: Sheela and Mona, the two incoming wives, break the household's solidarity and in a quarrel publicly announce Geeta as a widow, which deprives her of her place and of Mohan and sends her to her in-laws' house, where the article records that she is subjected to torments. The prohibition on a widow remarrying is the barrier underneath it.
lover_boy_explanation: Mohan follows the collapsing family to the village, takes work and becomes a singer to support it, and marries the widow the household discarded. The devotion is sustained and materially costly, though it is directed at the family as much as at Geeta.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The article's plot is written in unusually compressed and idiosyncratic English and states the relationship rather than showing it, so the bickering-lovers register has to be taken on its word.
actor_transformation: From one of four brothers in a shared house to the earner who supports the family and marries the widow it cast out.
female_transformation: From a child widow tolerated in her sister's household to a woman publicly denounced, sent away to be tormented, and finally married.
relationship_outcome: The article records the film ending with the marriage of Mohan and Geeta.
relationship_analysis: The third widow-remarriage plot of the career after Prem Rog (1982) and Deewana (1992), and the second in which Kapoor's character marries the widow himself. Placed beside Prem Rog it shows the same social barrier handled a decade later as domestic melodrama rather than as reform drama: the opposition here is two spiteful sisters-in-law rather than an armed aristocracy.
critical_reading: That Geeta is a child widow is stated and then used chiefly as ammunition for other women to deploy against her, which is a sharp observation about how such prohibitions actually operate. The film nonetheless gives her almost nothing to do: she is welcomed, denounced, expelled, tormented and finally married, in each case by someone else's decision.

initial_relationship: Performer and admirer; she is one of his followers
how_they_meet: Sagar is a well-known singer surrounded by female followers wherever he performs, and meets Sapna, one of them, in Srinagar; after some misunderstandings the two fall in love.
who_initiates: Sapna, as an admirer, before it becomes mutual
courtship_pattern: A holiday romance between a star and a follower, settled quickly into a decision to marry, and destroyed by an arrangement neither of them knew existed.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and confident, then severed by two families' prior commitments.
pair_conflict: None between them; the obstruction is entirely her father's arrangement.
pair_friction_explanation: The article records misunderstandings before the attachment forms and no conflict after it. The separation is imposed, and the couple's later meeting finds both of them promised elsewhere rather than at odds.
external_opposition_explanation: Sapna's father Narang has already arranged her marriage to Rakesh, the only son of Ranveer Singh, who is Sagar's own childhood friend. The obligation therefore runs in two directions at once, and the couple separate as a result.
lover_boy_explanation: A singer-hero whose whole plot is a romance, with the songs and the devotion that implies. The score stops short of the upper band because he responds to losing her by announcing a marriage of his own rather than by fighting for her, and because the article withholds the ending.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The article's plot is four sentences long and explicitly reserves the outcome for the climax, so the relationship is available only in outline.
actor_transformation: From a bachelor performer to a man engaged to one woman while in love with another.
female_transformation: From an admirer who won the singer to a daughter engaged to the man her father chose.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article states only that what happens to the love story forms the climax.
relationship_analysis: The obstacle here is doubled in a way that is unusual in the filmography: the rival is not merely wealthy but the son of the hero's own childhood friend, so the arrangement carries a claim of friendship as well as of paternal authority. The film's structure then gives Sagar a second engagement of his own, which is scored separately.
critical_reading: The premise, a famous singer and the follower who wins him, gives Sapna her position by admiration rather than by anything else, and the plot then transfers her between two families without her participation. The article's refusal to state the ending makes it impossible to say whether the film grants her a choice at the close.

initial_relationship: Not documented
how_they_meet: Not documented; Sagar announces his marriage to Kavita after Sapna is engaged to Rakesh.
who_initiates: Sagar, as a response to losing Sapna
courtship_pattern: None documented. The engagement is announced rather than arrived at, and the article gives it as a counter-move to Sapna's.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented; whatever feeling exists in the relationship appears to be hers, since his is directed elsewhere.
pair_conflict: He is in love with another woman and the engagement is a response to losing her.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is recorded, but the relationship is founded on his attachment to someone else. Scored provisionally: the article gives the engagement one clause and does not follow it.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is Sagar's own continuing love for Sapna rather than anything ranged against him and Kavita.
lover_boy_explanation: In this relationship Kapoor's character is contracting a marriage he does not want in order to answer a loss, which has none of the archetype's courtship, devotion or sacrifice.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, and the article documents almost nothing of it beyond the announcement. There is not enough recorded interaction to judge.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article reserves the resolution for the climax.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the article states the engagement as one of the two romantic positions the climax has to resolve. It belongs with Yeh Ishq Nahin Aasaan (1984) among the small group of films in which a Kapoor character enters a second marriage while still attached to the first woman, and in both cases the second woman is the one the film examines least.
critical_reading: Kavita exists to be the alternative, and the article gives her neither a courtship nor a response to being chosen as a consolation. Whether the film ultimately treats her as a person or as a device cannot be determined from what is documented.

actress_character: Lalita, courting him under the name Shikha
initial_relationship: Strangers; she uses him as cover while in hiding
how_they_meet: Lalita escapes JB on her wedding day, flees the city, and meets Raj, whom she at first uses as a cover under the assumed name Shikha; both then fall in love.
courtship_pattern: Built on her false name and her need for concealment, and formalised quickly when Raj's grandfather Rai Sahib arranges the wedding.
emotional_dynamic: Her calculation converting into genuine attachment, with him unaware of what she is hiding from.
pair_conflict: She is courting him under an assumed identity and concealing a man who considers her his property.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no quarrel between them, and the concealment is self-protective rather than exploitative. The friction is the undisclosed past, which JB exposes rather than she.
external_opposition_explanation: JB decided he must have Lalita, paid her uncle Madhi to arrange the marriage, kidnapped her when she refused and watched her daily until the wedding. After she escapes he traces her through her mother, exposes her identity to Raj and Rai Sahib with her uncle's help, and takes her back to be a dutiful wife on his terms.
lover_boy_explanation: Raj courts her, secures his grandfather's blessing, and finally kills the man holding her as he tries to kill her. The devotion is real and decisive, and falls short of the top band only because the film is structurally Madhuri Dixit's and his function for much of it is to be the safe place she reaches.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The second of three Kapoor and Madhuri Dixit films in four years; the relationship has to read as refuge rather than as conquest, which is a different register from his earlier romantic leads and suits the older man he was by then playing.
actor_transformation: From a man courting a woman under a name that is not hers to the one who kills her captor.
female_transformation: From a woman kidnapped and watched until her wedding day to one who engineers her own escape, builds a second identity, and is finally freed by force.
relationship_outcome: Raj kills JB as he tries to kill Lalita, and the two marry.
relationship_analysis: Structurally the clearest inversion of Badaltey Rishtey (1978) in the whole filmography. There Kapoor played the suitor whose pursuit turned into a standing threat against a married woman; here the obsessive pursuer is the villain and Kapoor is the refuge, and the film treats the behaviour it once gave him as grounds for killing. Read as a pair, the two films measure how the persona's relation to coercion changed across seventeen years.
critical_reading: The film is unambiguous that JB's conduct, buying a bride from her uncle, kidnapping her and calling permanent confinement being a dutiful wife, is monstrous, and it gives Lalita the intelligence to escape it herself rather than waiting to be rescued. Her deception of Raj is treated as reasonable self-protection, which is a notable shift from the films of the 1970s in which a woman courted under a false name was the joke.

initial_relationship: Strangers of different castes
how_they_meet: Somen meets Kajri at the annual festival and is immediately drawn to her despite her lower caste status; the article records that they fall in love and then part unexpectedly.
courtship_pattern: Two courtships separated by a year and a catastrophe: an immediate festival attraction, then a second approach at his uncle's dairy farm to a woman who now has a reason to evade him and cannot say it aloud.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and open at first; afterwards her love is intact and unspeakable, and his is confident and uninformed.
pair_conflict: She cannot tell him she was raped and bore and buried a child, and when his father discloses it at their engagement he walks out.
pair_friction_explanation: The decisive rupture is his: told at the engagement that Kajri had asked his father to cremate a child whose father she could not name, Somen leaves. He had not read the letter in which she explained it, and he returns only after his uncle shows it to him. That failure sits between the partners rather than outside them.
external_opposition_explanation: Her lower caste status, his father's orthodoxy as head priest, the rape by Roop Sahai that leaves her pregnant, a priest who refuses to cremate her dead infant, an aunt who wants to marry her to a shoemaker, and the village order that ostracises an unwed mother. Kedarnath, who burns a woman alive to protect the same man, marks how far that order will go.
lover_boy_explanation: Somen courts across caste, defies his father on principle and finally acts with Kajri against her rapist, which is substantial. The score is held down because the film's central test of his devotion is one he fails: he abandons her at the engagement on his father's word, without having read her account.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The third Kapoor and Madhuri Dixit film, and the demand on the pairing is unusual: for most of the second half she is playing concealment and he is playing an ignorance the audience can see through.
actor_transformation: From a man confident in his own progressivism to one who discovers he abandoned her at the first real test of it, and has to be brought back by a letter and his uncle.
female_transformation: From a village girl in love to a rape survivor who bears a child alone, begs so she can feed it, buries it when it dies, and finally names her attacker and acts against him.
relationship_outcome: Not documented in full; Kajri identifies Roop Sahai as the rapist and she, Somen and her father Baliram burn him.
relationship_analysis: The deliberate counterpart to Prem Rog fourteen years earlier, and the more honest of the two. Both films pair Kapoor with a woman destroyed by a sexual violation and a social order that blames her; in 1982 Devdhar rebuilds her life against an armed aristocracy, while here Somen walks out at the engagement. Directed by his younger brother Rajiv Kapoor, it is the film that tests the reform-hero persona and finds it conditional.
critical_reading: The film's treatment of Kajri is unusually unflinching for mainstream Hindi cinema of 1996: she is raped by a stranger, refused a cremation for her infant by a priest, driven out as an unwed mother, and it never suggests any of it is her fault. What it does with Somen is sharper still, since his walking out is presented as a real failure rather than a misunderstanding. The letter device, an explanation written and then not read, does let him off more lightly than his conduct warrants.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is a wife in hiding and he does not know it
how_they_meet: Priya escapes her violent husband Vikram during a storm on a boat, swims ashore and runs to Shimla, where she meets Raj Malhotra.
who_initiates: Raj, persistently enough that she tires of being followed
courtship_pattern: A pursuit she keeps deflecting, then an attempt at honesty that miscarries: her mother tells her to reveal the marriage and let him choose, and the letter she writes is lost and replaced with a poem, so he learns the truth from the wrong source and leaves.
emotional_dynamic: His open courtship against her withdrawal, and after the letter finally reaches him, a decision taken with full knowledge.
pair_conflict: She is married and cannot say so, and when he finds out by another route he abandons her.
pair_friction_explanation: Raj leaves her on discovering she is married, which is a real rupture and his own act, though it is produced by a letter going astray rather than by any bad faith on either side. He returns once he has her account, and the couple is united from then on.
external_opposition_explanation: Vikram is a suspicious and violently abusive husband who beat Priya, murdered the doctor who treated her and tried to help her blind mother, and believed her drowned. When he finds her picture in a newspaper he comes to Shimla, tries to kill Raj, has him imprisoned on a false charge of attempted murder, kills Priya's friend and attempts to kill her.
lover_boy_explanation: Raj courts persistently, chooses her knowing she is another man's wife, is imprisoned on a false charge for it and finally kills Vikram to save her. The devotion is unambiguous; the score is short of the top band because the film is a thriller in which the villain, not the lover, drives every turn.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The seventh of eleven Kapoor and Juhi Chawla films, and the part asks him to be the steady alternative to a young man's violence, which is where his screen presence had settled by the mid-1990s.
actor_transformation: From a suitor deterred by the discovery of a marriage to a man who marries her anyway and kills her husband to keep her alive.
female_transformation: From a battered wife who escapes by swimming ashore to a woman who insists on telling the truth before accepting a second man, and who tries to save even Vikram at the end.
relationship_outcome: Raj clears himself, drowns Vikram in a bathtub, and survives the final attack at the railway station where Vikram is killed by a train.
relationship_analysis: The second film in two years, after Yaraana, to cast Kapoor as the safe attachment against a violent prior claim on the heroine, and by 1996 that had become his settled position in a romance. It is also the exact inverse of Deewana four years earlier, where he was the first husband whose survival threatened a second marriage; here he is the second man and the first husband is the monster.
critical_reading: The film's account of domestic violence is direct and its sympathies are not in doubt, and Priya's insistence on disclosing her marriage before accepting Raj gives her a moral initiative the plot then frustrates through pure accident. Vikram's dying line, freeing her from all bonds as the train takes him, is the one false note: it grants an abuser a redemptive exit the rest of the film has earned no reason to give him.

actress_character: Dr. Sapna Mathur, also credited as Madhu Mathur
initial_relationship: Investigating officer and murder suspect
how_they_meet: Karan Saxena is assigned to apprehend the killer of a fellow officer, and the killer is Dr. Sapna Mathur; he arrests her and obtains a taped confession.
who_initiates: Karan, whose professional interest becomes personal
courtship_pattern: There is no courtship. The relationship develops through his refusal to close a case he has already won, and is consummated as an act of law-breaking when he helps her escape a death sentence.
emotional_dynamic: An officer's intrigue turning into attachment to a woman he himself convicted.
pair_conflict: He arrested her and secured the confession that condemned her.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no quarrel recorded, but the relationship's foundation is that he is the man who put her under sentence of death. That asymmetry sits inside the pair, though the film treats it as the reason for his devotion rather than as a division.
external_opposition_explanation: A death sentence handed down despite his efforts, a police manhunt launched for them both after he helps her escape, a conspiracy reaching into the state's chief minister and Karan's own friends, and a mysterious adversary following him everywhere.
lover_boy_explanation: Karan destroys his own career and becomes a fugitive for a woman under sentence of death, which is sacrifice on the archetype's scale. The register is investigative rather than romantic, though: there is no courtship, no songs of pursuit and no rival, and the film is a thriller throughout.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The fifth and last Kapoor and Sridevi film, after Nagina, Chandni, Banjaran and Gurudev, and the only one in which the relationship is conducted almost entirely across an interrogation and a prison rather than in song.
actor_transformation: From the officer who secured her conviction to a fugitive who broke his own case open and is hunted for it.
female_transformation: From a woman who confessed to murder and was sentenced to death to an escapee whose case turns out to implicate people in power.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article ends with neither of them knowing what will happen next.
relationship_analysis: The barrier here is unique in the filmography: not a family, a class or a religion but a conviction, a death sentence and the hero's own duty, which he abandons. It is the last of the five Sridevi pairings and the furthest from the register of the first, Nagina, where he was the ordinary man protected by a supernatural wife.
critical_reading: The film's premise, an officer who cannot accept the confession he himself extracted, is a genuinely interesting one and it treats Sapna's guilt as a question rather than a given. What it does not examine is the power he holds over her throughout: she is in custody, then condemned, then dependent on him for her escape, and the article records no point at which the relationship is negotiated between equals.

initial_relationship: Strangers courted by two friends at once
how_they_meet: Not documented in detail; the article records that Amar and the wealthy Rajiv Sinha, childhood friends with similar tastes, coincidentally fall in love with the same woman.
courtship_pattern: A rivalry conducted as friendship: Rajiv invents a pretext to talk Amar out of the marriage rather than compete openly, and Amar marries her in spite of it.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and firm on Amar's side, and undermined by a friend operating behind it.
pair_conflict: None between them; Amar is adamant and marries her.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Amar and Seema is recorded. The pressure is Rajiv's manipulation, and Amar's resistance to it is what makes the marriage happen.
external_opposition_explanation: Rajiv is wealthy, is Amar's closest friend, wants the same woman, and invents a pretext designed to separate them; when Amar learns what the pretext was for, the friendship becomes open enmity and Rajiv is later charged with killing a girl.
lover_boy_explanation: Amar marries her against a deliberate attempt to talk him out of it, which is a real romantic assertion, and the film's second half is his retaliation for it. The score sits mid-scale because there is no courtship dramatised and the plot converts quickly into a legal revenge.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, and the located review of the film is a retrospective one concerning its borrowing from Indecent Proposal. The eighth of eleven Kapoor and Juhi Chawla films.
actor_transformation: From a man who almost surrendered his marriage on a friend's word to a lawyer prosecuting that friend.
female_transformation: Not documented; the article gives Seema no action of her own.
relationship_outcome: They marry; the article's plot then follows the enmity and ends with Amar deciding to retaliate against Rajiv.
relationship_analysis: The last of the 1990s Juhi Chawla pairings and the thinnest, because the film's interest moves quickly from the marriage to the vendetta. Its one distinctive feature is that the rival tries to win by deceiving his friend rather than the woman, which keeps Seema outside the contest entirely.
critical_reading: Seema is the object of a rivalry she is never shown participating in: two men fall in love with her, one manipulates the other about her, and the article records no preference or action of hers at any point. The retrospective review's verdict, that the film added local twists to Indecent Proposal and failed, points at the same problem.

actress_prominence: Female lead of the parents' generation
initial_relationship: Married, and expecting a child when the film's action begins
how_they_meet: They do not meet in the film; the marriage is established and then destroyed in the opening movement.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The film is about a separation being undone twenty years later by the children it divided.
emotional_dynamic: A marriage ended on a manufactured suspicion, and two decades of separate lives on either side of it.
pair_conflict: He believes his stepsister's claim that Archana is having an affair, and they separate; by the time the twins intervene he is himself conducting an affair with Savitri.
pair_friction_explanation: The separation rests on his willingness to believe a lie about his wife without testing it, which is his failure, and the affair with Savitri is a second one. Both sit inside the marriage rather than outside it, even though the lie was planted.
external_opposition_explanation: Devyani, Raj's stepsister, wants his wealth and manufactures the accusation of infidelity that ends the marriage; the separation then divides the newborn twins between two countries, which keeps it in place for twenty years.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor plays the father in a twin-swap comedy: there is no courtship, and his romantic conduct in the film consists of believing a lie about his wife and taking up with another woman. The reconciliation is achieved by his daughters rather than by him.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The two are kept apart for almost the whole film by design and meet only at the close, so the relationship is carried by the children's efforts rather than by any interaction between the couple.
actor_transformation: From a husband who believed a lie to a father brought back to his wife by the daughters his suspicion separated.
female_transformation: From a wife accused of an affair she did not have to a woman who raised one daughter alone in London for twenty years.
relationship_outcome: Raj and Archana finally meet and consider living together again.
relationship_analysis: The last of the jealous-husband roles that run through Kapoor's 1990s work, from Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani onward, and the most lightly treated: here the suspicion is a comedy premise rather than a tragedy, and the reconciliation is a children's project. The structure is that of The Parent Trap grafted onto a Hindi family melodrama.
critical_reading: The film asks very little of Raj: he destroys his marriage on a lie, separates infant twins, conducts an affair, and is reunited with his wife by his daughters' ingenuity without having to account for any of it. Archana, who was falsely accused and raised a child alone, is the one who has to be brought round at the end.

initial_relationship: Married for years, with two daughters
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records only that Anwar and Rukhsana had been married for years.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The marriage exists in flashback and in the accusation that survives it.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented; an ambitious and popular singer on one side and a husband sinking into depression on the other.
pair_conflict: After the birth of their daughters he goes into depression and kills himself, and his elder daughter spends twenty years holding his wife responsible.
pair_friction_explanation: The article gives a depression and a suicide without explaining either, and sets them against a wife whose career was ascending. Scored in the middle band and provisionally: something in the marriage failed, and nothing located says what.
external_opposition_explanation: There is no external force acting on the marriage. What survives it is the family consequence: a court case, a daughter's grievance, and a household divided for years over a death the court had already ruled Rukhsana innocent of.
lover_boy_explanation: The part is a husband in a marriage the film examines only after his death, and the character's defining act is suicide. There is no courtship, devotion or sacrifice in the archetype's sense, and Kapoor appears largely in flashback.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, and the article records praise for Urmila Matondkar and Shabana Azmi rather than for the marriage scenes. The character exists in fragments, which leaves very little to judge.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the depression arrives after the daughters are born and the article offers no account of its course.
female_transformation: From a wife and ambitious singer to a widow accused by her own daughter of causing her husband's death, cleared in court and blamed anyway for twenty years.
relationship_outcome: Ended by his suicide; the film's disclosure is that he killed himself and Rukhsana was not responsible.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the marriage and its end are the question the whole film is built to answer, even though Kapoor's part in it is a special appearance conducted largely in flashback. It is the only pairing in the filmography that ends in the male character's suicide, and the only one whose central fact is a wrongful accusation levelled at the wife by her child.
critical_reading: The film, taken from Bergman's Autumn Sonata, is interested in what a daughter does with a grievance rather than in the marriage itself, and Anwar exists chiefly as the absence both women argue over. Its clearest statement is that a successful woman was blamed for her husband's death by everyone including a court that acquitted her, which the film treats as an injustice rather than a mystery.

initial_relationship: Strangers who meet in a street quarrel
how_they_meet: Walking his dogs across a busy intersection, Yash is nearly hit by a car, calls the police and berates the driver; Sheetal laughingly points out to the policeman that walking two dogs at once is itself against the law.
who_initiates: Neither; both go home and describe the quarrel to their families before they meet again
courtship_pattern: An adult courtship conducted openly and then in secret: a quarrel, a second meeting, a date at a Moroccan restaurant that is reported back to a gossiping acquaintance, and finally an elopement of two grandparents advised to run away together.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual, unhurried and companionable, grounded in what the two have in common rather than in pursuit: each has lost a spouse and each has put a family first.
pair_conflict: None of substance; the opening quarrel is the meeting rather than a division.
pair_friction_explanation: Yash and Sheetal are aligned from their second meeting onward. The comic hostility of the intersection scene is the film's way of introducing them, and no conflict between them follows it.
external_opposition_explanation: The opposition is their own adult children, who are irate about the relationship and suspect it of being a long-running secret affair conducted behind their backs. Madhu, the mother of Sheetal's prospective son-in-law, uses a report of their date as a further excuse to delay her son's wedding to Sheetal's daughter, so the romance is also a liability in a marriage negotiation.
lover_boy_explanation: Yash courts openly, runs away with her when the families object, and declares in front of both households that they intend to marry, which is the archetype's full sequence of pursuit, defiance and public declaration. It falls short of the top band because the register is companionship rather than ardour, and because the film gives him a retirement and a company to hand over as well.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, though the article records a reviewer noting Vikas Bhalla's comeback as Kapoor's son. The third Kapoor and Dimple Kapadia pairing, twenty years after Saagar and thirty-two after Bobby, and the film trades on that history: the ease between them is the premise rather than something the plot has to establish.
actor_transformation: From a man whose retirement is an absence of purpose to one who declares, in front of both families, that he intends to marry again.
female_transformation: From a widow organising her daughter's wedding and nothing of her own to a woman who leaves with him and is granted the marriage she wants.
relationship_outcome: Traced by the children after running away together, Yash declares their intention to marry and the families accept it; Sanju marries Riya.
relationship_analysis: The single most important pairing for the project's central question after Bobby, because it is the only one in which Kapoor plays the romantic lead of a conventional courtship while unambiguously being a parent. Every structural element of his 1970s romances is present, the near-zero pair friction, the external opposition, the elopement, the public declaration, with one inversion: the opposition comes from children rather than parents. Thirty-two years after Bobby, the same shape is played with the generations reversed, which is the clearest single measure of how the persona aged.
critical_reading: The film's most quietly radical move is treating two widowed parents' desire as legitimate and their children's embarrassment as the obstacle to be overcome, rather than the reverse. The children's suspicion that the relationship must be a long-standing secret affair is well observed, since it assumes older people could not simply have met. Sheetal is given the film's best line at the outset and a genuine choice at the end, though the declaration that settles matters is still his to make.

initial_relationship: Married in India before he emigrated
how_they_meet: Not documented; Manmohan married Bebo in India, went to London to establish himself, and obtained a visa for her four years later so that she could join him.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The marriage predates the film and what it dramatises is thirty years of one partner being quietly ashamed of the other.
emotional_dynamic: A settled marriage carried on across a humiliation that is never named: he is embarrassed by her and she knows it well enough to build her daughter a different life.
pair_conflict: He is embarrassed that she cannot speak English or mix with British people, and leaves her out of the occasions he attends while he socialises.
pair_friction_explanation: The article is explicit that Manmohan was always embarrassed by Bebo and as a firm result excluded her from important occasions. That is a sustained injury inside the marriage rather than an obstacle imposed on it, and it is entirely his doing.
external_opposition_explanation: The pressures are those of migration rather than of any person: four years apart while he established himself and she waited for a visa, and a British social world in which her lack of English made her, in his eyes, unpresentable.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no courtship, devotion or sacrifice in this relationship. Kapoor plays a husband whose treatment of his wife is the film's diagnosis of him, and the romantic energy in the film belongs entirely to the younger couple.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The marriage is established through Manmohan's conduct rather than through scenes between the two, and Nina Wadia's Bebo is given her weight by a single decision about her daughter rather than by any exchange with her husband.
actor_transformation: From a man embarrassed by his own wife to one confronted by a daughter who learned contempt for India exactly as he taught it.
female_transformation: From a wife excluded from her husband's social life to the parent who quietly determined that her daughter would not be treated as she was.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot follows Jasmeet's engagement rather than the marriage.
relationship_analysis: A marriage recorded not for its romance but for its diagnostic function: the film's whole argument about assimilation is contained in a husband who found his wife embarrassing, and in the daughter that shame produced. Female agency sits well above the relationship's other scores because Bebo's one documented act, educating Jasmeet in English so she would not end up as she had, is what sets the entire plot going.
critical_reading: The film is sharper about Manmohan than he is about himself: he wants an Indian son-in-law from a daughter he raised to be ashamed of India, having spent the marriage ashamed of an Indian wife. Bebo is given no scene in which she says any of this, which is both the portrait's realism and its limitation.

initial_relationship: Acquaintances in the same Old Delhi neighbourhood, many years before the film
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records only that Ali Beg fancied Roshan's mother Fatima many years ago, and that Roshan is surprised to learn it.
courtship_pattern: There is none. The attachment was never acted on, and its whole expression is a life left unmarried.
emotional_dynamic: One-sided and decades old, surviving as a fact the neighbourhood knows and Roshan does not.
pair_conflict: None recorded; she married elsewhere and he never married at all.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing between them is recorded as conflict. The relationship consists of a feeling that was never pressed, and the article treats it as part of the lane's history rather than as a quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is not documented directly, but Fatima married into the Mehra household and Ali Beg remained a Muslim bachelor in a lane the film shows sliding towards a religious dispute. Whatever kept them apart, it was decisive enough that he never married anyone.
lover_boy_explanation: A whole life's celibacy in consequence of one attachment is devotion on the archetype's scale, and it is the most romantic fact in the film. What holds the score down is that nothing is ever pursued, declared or sacrificed in the open; the devotion is entirely passive and entirely private.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The two characters share little or no screen time, since the attachment is delivered as a piece of neighbourhood knowledge rather than played out, so there is almost nothing between the performers to assess.
actor_transformation: None; the character is defined by a decision taken decades before the film and never revisited.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Never consummated; he has remained unmarried since, and the son of the woman he loved learns of it in passing.
relationship_analysis: Mutuality at one is the lowest score in the filmography, and deliberately so: this is the only pairing in which the relationship consists entirely of one person's unexpressed feeling across a lifetime. It is also among the most affecting of the late character roles, and a quiet late echo of Mera Naam Joker, where Kapoor first played a love that was never going to be returned.
critical_reading: The film treats Ali Beg's lifelong bachelorhood as a small dignified fact rather than a tragedy to be milked, which is why it lands. Fatima remains entirely a memory: she has no scene in which she acknowledges or even registers the attachment, so the reader is left with a man's fidelity to something the woman may never have known about.

actress_character: Harleen Kaur, later Harleen Kaur Panesar
actress_prominence: Female lead of the past-tense narrative, played by two actresses
initial_relationship: Strangers; he decides to marry her before they have spoken
how_they_meet: Veer sees Harleen and falls in love at first sight, pledging to marry her despite never having spoken to her; the whole courtship proceeds from that decision.
courtship_pattern: The old-fashioned pattern the film is built to defend: a silent devotion, a declaration made to her family rather than negotiated with her, and a persistence that survives being beaten for it.
emotional_dynamic: His certainty against her constrained position; she tells him to leave her when she learns she has been engaged elsewhere, and he does not accept it.
pair_conflict: She tells him he must leave her after discovering she was engaged without being consulted.
pair_friction_explanation: Her instruction to leave is made under her family's compulsion rather than out of any feeling against him, and he treats it as an obstacle rather than a refusal. Nothing divides the two by their own choice at any point.
external_opposition_explanation: Harleen's family engaged her to someone else without telling her, and when Veer declared his intention of marrying her they beat him badly for it. The opposition is physical and familial, and it is overcome only by his refusal to be deterred by it.
lover_boy_explanation: The purest lover-boy construction of the late career and the only other role besides Bobby and Laila Majnu to reach the top of the scale. Veer exists in the film precisely as an emblem of total romantic devotion: he commits to a woman before speaking to her, takes a beating from her family for saying so, and is still married to her half a century later. The film's entire thesis about love then and love now rests on him.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing specifically, though the article records warm notices for the performances generally. The casting is the point: Kapoor and his wife Neetu Kapoor play the couple in old age, with Saif Ali Khan and Giselli Monteiro as their younger selves, so the film borrows a real marriage of thirty years to authenticate the lifelong one it is asserting.
actor_transformation: None required in the frame story; the older Veer is already the finished argument, and the arc belongs to the young man he describes.
female_transformation: From a woman engaged without being consulted, who tells her suitor to go, to a wife of fifty years.
relationship_outcome: They marry and remain married; the older couple are together in the present-day frame, and Veer's account of it is what sends Jai back to Meera.
romantic_songs: 'Aahun Aahun', 'Yeh Dooriyan', 'Twist'
relationship_analysis: The most important pairing of the late career for the project's central question, because the film uses it explicitly as the standard against which modern love is measured: a man who decided, was beaten, and persisted, set against a couple who part amicably because their careers require it. It is also the clearest case in the filmography of the lover-boy archetype being handled as a historical object rather than inhabited, with Kapoor now playing the archetype's survivor while a younger star plays it live.
critical_reading: The film is knowingly nostalgic and mostly self-aware about it: Jai mocks Veer's ideals and the film lets the mockery stand even as it sides with him. What survives less well is Harleen, who is engaged without being told, tells Veer to leave, and is then won anyway; the romance the film holds up as exemplary is one in which the man's persistence overrides the woman's stated instruction, and it does not pause on that.

initial_relationship: Long married, with two teenage children
how_they_meet: Not documented; the marriage is decades old when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The film is a portrait of a working marriage under financial pressure, observed by the couple's daughter.
emotional_dynamic: Companionable and practical, conducted in a one-bedroom flat with two teenagers and no money, and capable of one partner overruling the other when family honour is at stake.
