pair_conflict: He says the car is impossible; she promises her sister-in-law they will come by car whatever it costs, which commits him to an expense he has already refused.
pair_friction_explanation: The one recorded disagreement is the car, and Kusum settles it by going over his head to reassure a distraught Urmi. Behind it sits a larger and quieter fact, that she gave up her job at his insistence, which the article states without dramatising.
external_opposition_explanation: The pressure is money and appearances: a teacher's salary, a one-bedroom flat, children whose expectations outrun the household, and a sister-in-law who will be taunted by her in-laws if the family arrives on a scooter.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no courtship or romantic gesture anywhere in the role. The register is entirely domestic, and what the part asks for is the texture of a long marriage rather than any expression of romantic love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The film casts Kapoor opposite his wife of more than thirty years in an unglamorous domestic register, and the ease between them is what the whole portrait rests on; it is the first of their films together to use the real marriage this way rather than for star value.
actor_transformation: From a man penny-pinching to stay respectable to one confronting what the pretence is costing his household.
female_transformation: Not documented within the film's action; the decisive fact about her, that she left her job because he wanted her to, is given as background.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot breaks off after the borrowed car is damaged on the return from Meerut.
relationship_analysis: The second of the four late films in which Kapoor plays a long-married man opposite Neetu Kapoor, after Love Aaj Kal the year before, and the one that established the register: no romance in the conventional sense, scored at three on both lover-boy and romance centrality, and yet among the most convincing relationships in the filmography. It marks the point at which his screen marriages stop being romantic and start being social observation.
critical_reading: The detail that Kusum quit her job at Santosh's insistence is dropped in without comment and quietly reframes the family's poverty as partly self-inflicted, which is the film's most acute touch. It is also the thing the film declines to examine: the household is short of money because one of two possible earners was withdrawn, and nobody in the film says so.

initial_relationship: Long married, with a large family in Southall
how_they_meet: Not documented; the marriage is decades old when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None shown. What the film examines is a wife's forty-year deference and the moment it ends.
emotional_dynamic: Submission on her side and unquestioned authority on his, until she says plainly what it has cost their children.
pair_conflict: She has spent the marriage acting only as his wife and not as a mother to her children, and finally tells him so while he has locked himself in the house.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no quarrel in the ordinary sense, but the film's turning point is Bebe telling Gurtej that she had never acted as a mother, only as a wife, and often forgot she was both. That is an indictment of the marriage delivered inside it, and it is what breaks his resistance.
external_opposition_explanation: Nothing opposes the marriage. What shaped it is the racism of an earlier generation in Britain, which formed Gurtej's authority and his refusal to let his son play for England, and which the people of Southall finally argue him out of.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is a patriarch, not a lover: there is no courtship, no devotion expressed to his wife, and his defining relationship in the film is with the son whose life he confiscated.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The fourth Kapoor and Dimple Kapadia pairing after Bobby, Saagar and Pyaar Mein Twist, and the only one in which they play a couple who have been married for decades; the film gives her the single speech that turns the plot, which is the whole of her leverage in the marriage.
actor_transformation: From a father who ruled by threat, including the threat of his own suicide, to a man who watches his son on television and asks to be driven to the ground to apologise.
female_transformation: From a wife who deferred for forty years to one who names what the deference cost, turns on the television against her husband's will, and is the immediate cause of his change.
relationship_outcome: The marriage survives and is the instrument of the reconciliation: Gurtej apologises to Gattu at the stadium and his other children are freed to follow their own ambitions.
relationship_analysis: The second of the late long-marriage portraits and the sharpest, because the film locates its whole resolution in a wife's belated refusal to keep deferring. Female agency at seven against mutuality at four is the most lopsided pairing in the late work, and the imbalance is the point: she has one decisive act in forty years and it is enough to end the film.
critical_reading: The film is unusually precise about how patriarchal authority is maintained by the compliance of the person closest to it, and Bebe's line about forgetting she was a mother as well as a wife is its best piece of writing. It is also generous to Gurtej in a way it need not be, tracing his tyranny to the racism he suffered and then letting a cricket match dissolve it.

initial_relationship: She left her husband and twelve-year-old daughter for him
how_they_meet: Not documented; the article records that Meera's mother left for another man when Meera was twelve, and that Kapoor's Imraan Sharqazi is Meera's step-father.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The relationship exists in the present as a settled household and in the past as the departure that defined Meera's childhood.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented; by the time of the film the two are established together and estranged from Meera.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them; the cost of the relationship was borne by the family Pooja left.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing between Imraan and Pooja is recorded as conflict. What the relationship generated is a twenty-year estrangement from her daughter, which is a consequence rather than a friction inside the pair.
external_opposition_explanation: The marriage exists on the far side of a broken one: Pooja left an affluent Punjabi household and a twelve-year-old child for it, and the daughter's refusal of her mother is the standing consequence until Samar engineers a reconciliation.
lover_boy_explanation: The part is a settled step-father in a special appearance, with no courtship, pursuit or declaration of any kind. Whatever romantic action the relationship required happened long before the film begins.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Neetu Kapoor appear together as the couple, both credited as special appearances, and the roles are small enough that the casting does more work than the writing.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: From a woman estranged from the daughter she left to one reconciled with her when Samar brings Meera to visit.
relationship_outcome: The marriage is intact, and the estrangement it produced is repaired when Meera and her mother reconcile.
relationship_analysis: The thinnest of the four late Neetu Kapoor pairings and recorded chiefly because the marriage is the fact Meera's whole character is built on: a mother who left, a step-father in her place, and twenty years of refusal. It is also the last film Yash Chopra directed, twenty-three years after he directed Kapoor in Chandni.
critical_reading: The film is notably unpunishing towards a woman who left a marriage and a child, allowing her a settled second relationship and a reconciliation rather than a reckoning, which is not what the convention would predict. Neither partner is given any account of the departure itself, so the relationship remains a premise rather than a portrait.

initial_relationship: Long married, and serving in the same police force
how_they_meet: Not documented; the two are established as a married pair of police officers when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The relationship is a working partnership in uniform, played for comedy.
emotional_dynamic: A double act: they investigate, arrest, take a bribe and change their minds as a single unit, and their childlessness is the fact the film finally turns on.
pair_conflict: None between them at any point.
pair_friction_explanation: The Chautalas are never at odds. They are corruptible together, confronted together, persuaded together and decide to adopt together, which makes this the most consistently aligned couple in the late filmography.
external_opposition_explanation: The hawala racketeer Chandel, who has kidnapped the orphanage children, and the case against Babli that the two of them are pursuing. Nothing is aimed at the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no courtship or romantic gesture in the role. The relationship is comic and companionable, and what the part asks for is a double act rather than any romantic register.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, though the article records a reviewer crediting the film's appeal to the power of three Kapoors. The comedy depends entirely on the two operating as one, and the real marriage behind it supplies the shorthand the writing does not.
actor_transformation: From a corruptible officer who takes the hawala money to a man who joins the raid and then adopts the thief he was chasing.
female_transformation: The same movement, taken jointly: from an officer accepting a bribe to a woman deciding, with her husband, to become a mother.
relationship_outcome: The childless couple decide to adopt Babli and to stop him being a thief.
relationship_analysis: Mutuality at eight is the highest reading among the late marriages, because the film gives the two characters no separate positions at all. Its real distinction is off-screen: this is the only film in which Kapoor appears with both his wife and his son, and the plot has the couple he plays half of decide to adopt the young man his own son is playing.
critical_reading: The film uses the Kapoor family as its own punchline, which the one positive review the article records acknowledges directly by crediting three Kapoors for whatever works. The childlessness that motivates the adoption is a device rather than a subject, and the couple's corruption is forgiven the moment they become sympathetic.

initial_relationship: Long married, and divorced by the time the film's action begins
how_they_meet: Not documented; the marriage and its end both precede the story Inder returns into.
courtship_pattern: None shown. What the film reveals, in stages, is why a marriage ended and why the man who ended it is not the villain his son takes him for.
emotional_dynamic: A marriage dismantled by illness and debt rather than by feeling, with the husband carrying reasons he does not explain and a wife who can no longer hold them.
pair_conflict: He divorced her and placed her in an ashram while she was losing her memory to Alzheimer's, and told his son none of the reasons.
pair_friction_explanation: The divorce and the ashram are his acts and they look, to everyone including his son, like abandonment of a sick wife. The film's turn is that there were deeper reasons and it was not his fault, but the friction inside the marriage is real and is what the plot exists to explain.
external_opposition_explanation: Her Alzheimer's, which is advanced enough that he signs a bank form on her behalf, and years of borrowing from Cheema that end in a ransom demand against the two of them.
lover_boy_explanation: No courtship or romantic expression is involved. The role is a husband managing an illness and a debt badly and in silence, and the reconciliation is arranged by his son rather than sought by him.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing. The illness means Supriya Pathak plays much of the part without access to the marriage's history, so the relationship has to be carried by his conduct towards her rather than by exchanges between them.
actor_transformation: From a father dismissed by his son as heartless to a man whose reasons are finally heard and whose marriage is restored to him.
female_transformation: Largely acted upon: divorced, sent to an ashram, signed for at a bank, and married again at her son's arrangement, with Alzheimer's removing her from each decision.
relationship_outcome: Inder pays off Cheema and has his parents married to each other again.
relationship_analysis: Female agency at two is the lowest score among the late marriages, and it is the illness rather than the film's attitude that produces it: Pammi is legally and practically unable to participate in any of the decisions taken about her. The pairing belongs with Do Dooni Chaar and Patiala House in the late run of long marriages, and is the only one in which the marriage has to be reconstituted rather than merely repaired.
critical_reading: The film's sympathy is organised entirely around the son's misjudgement of his father, so the wife with Alzheimer's functions as the evidence in a dispute between two men. Remarrying her at the close is offered as a happy resolution without the film pausing on whether she is in a position to consent to it.

initial_relationship: Strangers; both widowed, meeting at a kitty party he is catering
how_they_meet: Sharmaji, cooking for kitty parties to fill his forced retirement, befriends Veena Manchanda at the second such party; she is a boutique owner whose husband died in a car crash three years earlier.
who_initiates: Mutual, growing out of the parties he caters
courtship_pattern: Not a courtship in any declared sense. The article records the two bonding over the kitty parties and becoming close friends, which is as far as the documented relationship goes.
emotional_dynamic: Warm, easy and companionable between two people whose spouses are dead and whose families would rather they stayed quiet.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing between Sharmaji and Veena is recorded as conflict. The pressure in the film comes from his sons' humiliation at his dancing and his new life, not from anything in the friendship.
external_opposition_explanation: His sons are furious and humiliated when a video of him dancing at a kitty party circulates among the extended family, and the household is already strained by Rinku's concealed plan to move out. The disapproval is of his whole late-life reinvention rather than of Veena specifically.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no declaration, pursuit or romantic gesture on record, so the archetype's machinery is absent. What is present is the thing the archetype is ultimately about, a man organising his life around a person he has chosen, and he does it against his children's embarrassment, which is why the score sits at the middle rather than lower.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no located review assesses this pairing, though the article records several notices praising Kapoor's own performance, including Sukanya Verma of Rediff calling the film his swansong and show. Juhi Chawla's eleventh and last film with him, and the relationship's warmth is the film's principal pleasure.
actor_transformation: From a man forcibly retired at fifty-eight and bored into applying for odd jobs to one with a vocation, a circle and a companion, held against his sons' disapproval.
female_transformation: Not documented in detail; a widow running a boutique who gains a friend and, with her circle, gives him a place to be.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the article's plot breaks off in the family's dispute over Rinku's apartment, with the friendship established.
relationship_analysis: The last pairing of the filmography and a deliberate late counterpart to Pyaar Mein Twist seventeen years earlier: two widowed people finding each other against their grown children's embarrassment. Romance presence is recorded as Implied rather than Major because the article documents a friendship and stops there; the relationship is scored on what is written rather than on what the shape of the film invites, and the confidence grade reflects that.
critical_reading: The film's subject is a man permitted to want things again after retirement, and the friendship with Veena is the clearest instrument of that; the children's humiliation at a video of their father dancing is its sharpest observation. Whether the film ultimately makes the relationship romantic cannot be settled from what is documented, and it is recorded here as friendship with a romantic reading left open rather than asserted.
